title: What does the "yield" keyword do in Python?
body:
What functionality does the yield keyword in Python provide?

For example, I'm trying to understand this code1:

def _get_child_candidates(self, distance, min_dist, max_dist):
    if self._leftchild and distance - max_dist < self._median:
        yield self._leftchild
    if self._rightchild and distance + max_dist >= self._median:
        yield self._rightchild

And this is the caller:

result, candidates = [], [self]
while candidates:
    node = candidates.pop()
    distance = node._get_dist(obj)
    if distance <= max_dist and distance >= min_dist:
        result.extend(node._values)
    candidates.extend(node._get_child_candidates(distance, min_dist, max_dist))
return result

What happens when the method _get_child_candidates is called? Is a list returned? A single element? Is it called again? When will subsequent calls stop?

1. This piece of code was written by Jochen Schulz (jrschulz), who made a great Python library for metric spaces. This is the link to the complete source: Module mspace.

title: "Least Astonishment" and the Mutable Default Argument
body:
def foo(a=[]):
    a.append(5)
    return a

Python novices expect this function called with no parameter to always return a list with only one element: [5]. The result is different and astonishing:

>>> foo()
[5]
>>> foo()
[5, 5]
>>> foo()
[5, 5, 5]
>>> foo()
[5, 5, 5, 5]
>>> foo()

The behavior has an underlying explanation, but it is unexpected if you don't understand internals. What is the reason for binding the default argument at function definition, and not at function execution? I doubt the experienced behavior has a practical use (who really used static variables in C, without breeding bugs?)

Edit:

Baczek made an interesting example. Together with your comments and Utaal's in particular, I elaborated:

def a():
    print("a executed")
    return []

           
def b(x=a()):
    x.append(5)
    print(x)

a executed
>>> b()
[5]
>>> b()
[5, 5]

It seems that the design decision was relative to where to put the scope of parameters: inside the function, or "together" with it?

Doing the binding inside the function would mean that x is effectively bound to the specified default when the function is called, not defined, something that would present a deep flaw: the def line would be "hybrid" in the sense that part of the binding (of the function object) would happen at definition, and part (assignment of default parameters) at function invocation time.

The actual behavior is more consistent: everything of that line gets evaluated when that line is executed, meaning at function definition.

title: Why is "1000000000000000 in range(1000000000000001)" so fast in Python 3?
body:
It is my understanding that the range() function, which is actually an object type in Python 3, generates its contents on the fly, similar to a generator.

This being the case, I would have expected the following line to take an inordinate amount of time because, in order to determine whether 1 quadrillion is in the range, a quadrillion values would have to be generated:

1_000_000_000_000_000 in range(1_000_000_000_000_001)

Furthermore: it seems that no matter how many zeroes I add on, the calculation more or less takes the same amount of time (basically instantaneous).

I have also tried things like this, but the calculation is still almost instant:

# count by tens
1_000_000_000_000_000_000_000 in range(0,1_000_000_000_000_000_000_001,10)

If I try to implement my own range function, the result is not so nice!

def my_crappy_range(N):
    i = 0
    while i < N:
        yield i
        i += 1
    return

What is the range() object doing under the hood that makes it so fast?

Martijn Pieters's answer was chosen for its completeness, but also see abarnert's first answer for a good discussion of what it means for range to be a full-fledged sequence in Python 3, and some information/warning regarding potential inconsistency for __contains__ function optimization across Python implementations. abarnert's other answer goes into some more detail and provides links for those interested in the history behind the optimization in Python 3 (and lack of optimization of xrange in Python 2). Answers by poke and by wim provide the relevant C source code and explanations for those who are interested.

title: Why is reading lines from stdin much slower in C++ than Python?
body:
I wanted to compare reading lines of string input from stdin using Python and C++ and was shocked to see my C++ code run an order of magnitude slower than the equivalent Python code. Since my C++ is rusty and I'm not yet an expert Pythonista, please tell me if I'm doing something wrong or if I'm misunderstanding something.

(TLDR answer: include the statement: cin.sync_with_stdio(false) or just use fgets instead.

TLDR results: scroll all the way down to the bottom of my question and look at the table.)

C++ code:

#include <iostream>
#include <time.h>

using namespace std;

int main() {
    string input_line;
    long line_count = 0;
    time_t start = time(NULL);
    int sec;
    int lps;

    while (cin) {
        getline(cin, input_line);
        if (!cin.eof())
            line_count++;
    };

    sec = (int) time(NULL) - start;
    cerr << "Read " << line_count << " lines in " << sec << " seconds.";
    if (sec > 0) {
        lps = line_count / sec;
        cerr << " LPS: " << lps << endl;
    } else
        cerr << endl;
    return 0;
}

// Compiled with:
// g++ -O3 -o readline_test_cpp foo.cpp

Python Equivalent:

#!/usr/bin/env python
import time
import sys

count = 0
start = time.time()

for line in  sys.stdin:
    count += 1

delta_sec = int(time.time() - start_time)
if delta_sec >= 0:
    lines_per_sec = int(round(count/delta_sec))
    print("Read {0} lines in {1} seconds. LPS: {2}".format(count, delta_sec,
       lines_per_sec))

Here are my results:

$ cat test_lines | ./readline_test_cpp
Read 5570000 lines in 9 seconds. LPS: 618889

$ cat test_lines | ./readline_test.py
Read 5570000 lines in 1 seconds. LPS: 5570000

I should note that I tried this both under Mac OS X v10.6.8 (Snow Leopard) and Linux 2.6.32 (Red Hat Linux 6.2). The former is a MacBook Pro, and the latter is a very beefy server, not that this is too pertinent.

$ for i in {1..5}; do echo "Test run $i at `date`"; echo -n "CPP:"; cat test_lines | ./readline_test_cpp ; echo -n "Python:"; cat test_lines | ./readline_test.py ; done

title: How do I declare custom exceptions in modern Python?
body:
How do I declare custom exception classes in modern Python? My primary goal is to follow whatever standard other exception classes have, so that (for instance) any extra string I include in the exception is printed out by whatever tool caught the exception.

By "modern Python" I mean something that will run in Python 2.5 but be 'correct' for the Python 2.6 and Python 3.* way of doing things. And by "custom" I mean an Exception object that can include extra data about the cause of the error: a string, maybe also some other arbitrary object relevant to the exception.

I was tripped up by the following deprecation warning in Python 2.6.2:

>>> class MyError(Exception):
...     def __init__(self, message):
...         self.message = message
... 
>>> MyError("foo")
_sandbox.py:3: DeprecationWarning: BaseException.message has been deprecated as of Python 2.6

It seems crazy that BaseException has a special meaning for attributes named message. I gather from PEP-352 that attribute did have a special meaning in 2.5 they're trying to deprecate away, so I guess that name (and that one alone) is now forbidden? Ugh.

I'm also fuzzily aware that Exception has some magic parameter args, but I've never known how to use it. Nor am I sure it's the right way to do things going forward; a lot of the discussion I found online suggested they were trying to do away with args in Python 3.

For a complicated project environment, with tons of different directories, this can take around 5 seconds -- all to run a script that might fail instantly.

title: Trying to get a list from pyodbc.drivers(), but it produces nothing why?
body:
Trying to setup a simple ODBC project. To make sure I name the correct driver in the connection, I wanted to have pyodbc report the current drivers.

Is pyodbc.drivers() supposed to report this information, or is there more to do after the call to see the list of drivers?

Windows 10 VSCode python 3.7.2 64-bit no virtual environment python freeze reports pyodbc==4.0.30 (& also 4.0.27)

Windows ODBC Data Source Administrator both (32 & 64 bit) show many drivers. MS Excel is working with PostgreSQL.

import pyodbc
Print("List of ODBC drivers:")
pyodbc.drivers()
print("End of List")

Just gives terminal output:

List of ODBC drivers:
End of List

Initially, import pyodbc was causing an exception. Un-installed pyodbc, rebooted, re-installed, that seemed to sort the exceptions out, but not the results I was looking for. Tried going back to pyodbc 4.0.27 no change

Edited, because I sorted it out:

The answer is that, yes there is more to do. pyodbc.drivers() returns a list To get the driver names, I needed to do:

import pyodbc
print("List of ODBC Drivers:")
dlist = pyodbc.drivers()
for drvr in dlist:
    print(drvr)

print("End of List")

And I now get:

List of ODBC Drivers:
SQL Server
QB SQL Anywhere
Transoft 64 bit ODBC Driver
PostgreSQL ODBC Driver(ANSI)
PostgreSQL ODBC Driver(UNICODE)
End of List

Which is what I needed.

The list only contains the 64 bit drivers, because I'm using 64 bit python.

n = index/scaling_factor

Rounded down to the nearest integer, so that it is a valid index position:

n = math.floor(index/scaling_factor)

In the example code below, the scaling factor fed to the function first_n_elements is 2.

For example, let's say I have the sentence "I like cheese" at index position 225. Let's say n = index/2 rounded down to the nearest integer, which would be 112.

Since its earliest days, Python allowed dynamically importing modules via builtins.__import__():

np = __import__('numpy')

Although this is now discouraged in favour of importlib.import_module().

Python 3.15 introduced lazy imports, with new lazy import and lazy from syntax:

lazy import numpy as np

Is there an equivalent to __import__() or import_module() to dynamically and lazily import modules?

(I've been here and here, but there's no mention of a dynamic mechanism. And the builtin functions page only mentions __import__().)

title: How to build Pip RPM from bootstrap using tarball/wheel?
body:
I am packaging pip v26.2.2 as an RPM (python311-pip) to be installed inside a custom, isolated prefix.

The target build environment is a completely clean, offline Docker container that lacks a pre-installed system pip, external package index access, or pre-packaged PEP 517 build backends.

Environment Reproducer (Dockerfile)

To illustrate the exact constraints, here is a minimal reproduction of the clean Docker build environment:

FROM rockylinux:9-minimal

# Setup isolated custom Python 3.11 prefix and minimal build tools
RUN microdnf install -y rpm-build rpmdevtools dnf-plugins-core \
    python311 python311-devel python311-setuptools \
    pyproject-rpm-macros python3-rpm-generators zip unzip && \
    microdnf clean all

WORKDIR /build

The Problem & Reference Spec Discrepancies

While older enterprise RPM specs for Python 3.11 python-pip relied on deprecated legacy setup.py build paths, modern versions have migrated strictly to PEP 517 compliance governed by pyproject.toml (utilizing flit_core as its build backend).

When examining modern reference implementations—such as CentOS Stream's and AlmaLinux's python3.14-pip.spec on c10s—they leverage modern RPM macros (%pyproject_wheel, %pyproject_install, %pyproject_save_files).

However, adopting these macros inside our strictly isolated offline container introduces a circular bootstrapping dependency:

Modern build macros and frontends internally invoke pip or build tools (python3-build, python3-installer) to compile packages.

Because our target custom prefix and buildroot lack a pre-installed system pip or package index access, standard macro execution fails.

Our build constraints strictly limit us to using only python311-devel, python311-setuptools, pyproject-rpm-macros, python3-rpm-generators, and basic archiving utilities (zip/unzip).

When attempting to build the pip wheel using:

%{\__python3} -m flit_core.wheel --outdir dist

It fails because flit_core is not present in the clean environment. However, my build constraints strictly limit me to using only python311-devel, python311-setuptools, pyproject-rpm-macros, python3-rpm-generators, and basic archiving utilities (zip/unzip). I cannot rely on a pre-existing host pip to install build-time dependencies.

I've tried:

  1. Downloading flit_core as a secondary source (Source1): I successfully unpack flit_core alongside pip during %prep and export its src/ path to PYTHONPATH.

  2. Extracting wheels manually: I tried building flit_core locally into a staging folder and extracting its .whl archive via Python’s zipfile module to avoid calling pip install (since pip isn't installed yet).

Given this strictly isolated offline container setup and the explicit set of available build dependencies, how can we properly bootstrap and orchestrate flit_core as a local build backend during the rpmbuild %build phase to successfully generate and install the pip wheel into our custom prefix, bridging the gap between legacy specs and modern PEP 517 macro workflows?

title: Implementing rate limiting with dynamic quotas based on user subscription level in FastAPI with Redis
body:
I'm building an API that needs to handle different rate limits based on user subscription levels (free, premium, enterprise). I'm using FastAPI with Redis for rate limiting, but struggling with implementing dynamic quotas. Current implementation:

from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, HTTPException
import redis
from typing import Optional

app = FastAPI()
redis_client = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0)

async def get_rate_limit(user_id: str) -> int:
    # Currently hardcoded, need dynamic solution
    return 100  # requests per hour

@app.get("/api/data")
async def get_data(user_id: str = Depends(get_current_user)):
    quota = await get_rate_limit(user_id)
    # Rate limiting logic here

How can I:

  1. Implement dynamic quotas that update when user changes subscription
  2. Handle burst requests efficiently
  3. Implement a sliding window rather than fixed window
  4. Provide users with remaining quota information
  5. Handle distributed environment scenarios

I've looked at various rate limiting algorithms but unsure about best practices for dynamic quotas in a distributed system.

What I tried:

  1. Implemented basic Redis-based rate limiting:
async def check_rate_limit(user_id: str) -> bool:
    key = f"rate_limit:{user_id}"
    current = await redis_client.incr(key)
    if current == 1:
        await redis_client.expire(key, 3600)  # 1 hour expiry
    return current <= await get_rate_limit(user_id)
  1. Added subscription-based quotas:
QUOTA_MAPPING = {
    'free': 100,
    'premium': 1000,
    'enterprise': 5000
}

async def get_rate_limit(user_id: str) -> int:
    subscription = await get_user_subscription(user_id)
    return QUOTA_MAPPING.get(subscription, 100)
  1. Attempted sliding window implementation:
async def check_sliding_window(user_id: str):
    now = time.time()
    window_start = now - 3600  # 1 hour window
    
    pipeline = redis_client.pipeline()
    pipeline.zadd(f"requests:{user_id}", {now: now})
    pipeline.zremrangebyscore(f"requests:{user_id}", 0, window_start)
    pipeline.zcard(f"requests:{user_id}")
    results = await pipeline.execute()
    
    return results[2] <= await get_rate_limit(user_id)

Expected:

  • Smooth handling of quota updates when subscription changes
  • Accurate tracking in distributed environment
  • Proper sliding window implementation without memory leaks
  • Efficient handling of burst requests

Actual results:

  • Race conditions when updating quotas
  • Memory usage grows unbounded with sliding window implementation
  • Burst requests cause Redis performance issues
  • Distributed systems face synchronization problems

title: Why does ContextVar return its default value inside run_in_executor() in Python asyncio?
body:
I'm working on an asynchronous Python application where I use ContextVar to store request-specific information, such as a request ID. This allows me to access the current request ID from different functions without passing it as an argument everywhere.

import asyncio
from contextvars import ContextVar

request_id = ContextVar("request_id", default="missing")


def read_request_id():
    return request_id.get()


async def main():
    token = request_id.set("request-123")

    try:
        print("Inside async function:", request_id.get())

        loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()

        result = await loop.run_in_executor(
            None,
            read_request_id
        )

        print("Inside executor:", result)

    finally:
        request_id.reset(token)


asyncio.run(main())

The value works correctly inside my asynchronous functions, but when I execute a synchronous function using loop.run_in_executor(), the function receives the default value instead of the value set by the current request:

Inside async function: request-123
Inside executor: missing

I want:

Inside async function: request-123
Inside executor: request-123

I understand that run_in_executor() executes the function in a separate thread. However, I expected the current execution context to be available to the submitted function, since the ContextVar is already set in the calling asynchronous task.

I also need to use a preconfigured ThreadPoolExecutor in my actual application, so simply replacing run_in_executor() with asyncio.to_thread() is not necessarily an option.

What is the correct and thread-safe way to propagate the current Context when submitting a synchronous function through loop.run_in_executor(), particularly when using a custom ThreadPoolExecutor, without manually passing every ContextVar value as an argument?

title: Benchmarking Python Decorator Overhead
body:
I am working on the project Type Enforced which is a framework for enforcing python type hints using a decorator. I am trying to benchmark this project vs other fast frameworks like Beartype. Essentially, the overhead for initializing a function is far greater than the overhead of adding the decorator.

In this sense, I have been taking the differential of execution time between the decorated function time and the undecorated function time averages.

Now, these differential measurements are falling at about 10 ns for Type Enforced vs about 200 ns for Beartype on basic validations like:

def my_fn_vanilla(a:int):
    pass

@type_enforced.Enforcer
def my_fn_te(a:int):
    pass

@beartype
def my_fn_bt(a:int):
    pass

Essentially, I run each of these functions n times and take the average time of running them. I then subtract the average of n runs for:

te_diff = avg_time_my_fn_te - avg_time_my_fn_vanilla
bt_diff = avg_time_my_fn_bt - avg_time_my_fn_vanilla

Such that I can compare the additional apples to apples on added overhead since just running the vanilla function takes about 5000 ns while the added overhead for type_enforced and beartype are about 10 ns and 200 ns respectively.

These timings are pretty stable at smaller and larger sizes of timing samples and across system architectures (relative to processor and memory yada yada - but still relative on orders of magnitude).

My concern stems from the fact that we are measuring python in terms of 20 clock cycles of differential. Assuming there are no bug in the code or measurements, is this something that can be trusted?

I am looking for some holes in the methodology that I should be checking for and potential edge cases I may be missing. Are there documented other ways that this can be measured / benchmarked / tested?

Related to a previous post: https://codereview.stackexchange.com/questions/302938/benchmarking-type-hint-validation-in-python/302948#302948 . Note that recent speedups in the framework are driving this new thread of questions.

title: Do proxy credentials containing @ or : need percent-encoding in requests' proxies dict, and is quote(safe="") correct?
body:
I'm sending HTTPS requests through an authenticated HTTP proxy with the Requests library. The password contains @ and :, which are reserved characters in a URL's userinfo part.

import requests

from urllib.parse import quote

user = "user"

password = "p@ss:word"          # example value, contains @ and :

host = "proxy.example.com:8080"

proxy_url = f"http://{quote(user, safe='')}:{quote(password, safe='')}@{host}"

proxies = {

    "http": proxy_url,

    "https": proxy_url,

}

r = requests.get("https://httpbin.org/ip", proxies=proxies, timeout=10)

print(r.status_code, r.text)

The same URL can also be supplied through the environment instead of the proxies argument:

export HTTPS_PROXY='http://user:p%40ss%3Aword@proxy.example.com:8080'

python script.py

My understanding is this:

  1. Without encoding, p@ss:word makes the URL ambiguous, because everything after the last @ is read as the host.

  2. With quote(password, safe=''), the string becomes p%40ss%3Aword.

  3. Requests is supposed to percent-decode the userinfo again before it builds the Proxy-Authorization: Basic ... header for the CONNECT request.

I could not find this stated explicitly in the Requests documentation. I only want to rely on it if it is guaranteed behavior and not an accident of the current implementation.

When credentials are embedded in a proxy URL passed to Requests (via proxies= or HTTPS_PROXY), does Requests unquote them before sending Proxy-Authorization, and is urllib.parse.quote(value, safe='') the right way to encode them?

I'm also interested in whether the answer differs between the proxies= argument and the environment variables, since both go through different code paths in Session.

Environment: Python 3, Requests v2.x, urllib3 v2.x, HTTP proxy that requires Basic authentication.

    await asyncio.sleep(1 if version == 0 else 0.2)
    return f"{key}-v{version}"

async def get_data(key):
    version = versions.get(key, 0)

    if key in cache:
        return cache[key]

    if key not in pending:
        pending[key] = asyncio.create_task(fetch(key, version))

    task = pending[key]

    try:
        result = await task
        cache[key] = result
        return result
    finally:
        pending.pop(key, None)

async def invalidate(key):
    cache.pop(key, None)
    versions[key] = versions.get(key, 0) + 1

async def main():
    first = asyncio.create_task(get_data("user-1"))

    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    await invalidate("user-1")

    second = asyncio.create_task(get_data("user-1"))

    results = await asyncio.gather(first, second)

    print(results)
    print(cache)

asyncio.run(main())

What I'm not sure about is what should happen when the second request comes in after invalidation but the first fetch is still running.

Should the second request wait for the existing task, or should it start a new fetch using the updated version?

If both requests are allowed to run independently, how do I prevent the older task from writing stale data into the cache when it eventually finishes?

Also, can the finally block cause problems when multiple callers are sharing the same task, particularly if one caller finishes before another?

What's the best way to handle this without introducing race conditions?

title: High volume URL parsing in Python
body:
I use the polars, urllib and tldextract packages in python to parse 2 columns of URL strings in zstd-compressed parquet files (averaging 8GB, 40 million rows). The parsed output include the scheme, netloc, subdomain, domain, suffix, path, query, and fragment. On my PC, processing a single file takes about 16 minutes (64GB RAM, 32 logical cores). Input data is read from one SSD (x:/) and output is written to a separate SSD (y:/).

My code doesn't use multiprocessing. It relies on polars' streaming and vectorization features for efficiency. RAM usage is near the limit when processing. I don't get the full benefit of polars' vectorization since urllib and tldextract are not native to polars' engine (rust).

Are there alternative approaches or modifications that would help speed processing? Is 16 minute processing time reasonable? I've considered creating a Rust extension for polars that has the same functionality of urllib and tldextract but that seems like reinventing the wheel.

The method below does the heavy lifting (python 3.12, polars 1.31)

def build_parsed_url_for_date(
    event_date: str,
    silver_root: Path,
    gold_root: Path,
    compression: str = "zstd",
) -> None:
    """
    For a given event_date (YYYY-MM-DD):

    - Read SILVER parquet from: silver_root / f"event_date={event_date}" / *.parquet
    - Parse `url` and `referrer` columns into components (PSL-based).
    - Write GOLD/parsed_url parquet to:
          gold_root / "parsed_url" / f"event_date={event_date}" / "part.parquet"
    """
    # input paths
    silver_partition = silver_root / f"event_date={event_date}"
    if not silver_partition.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"SILVER partition not found: {silver_partition}")

    silver_files = sorted(silver_partition.glob("*.parquet"))
    if not silver_files:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"No parquet files in {silver_partition}")


    # polars lazy frame
    lf = pl.scan_parquet([str(f) for f in silver_files])

    # wrappers for urllib and tldextract parsers
    parser_url = make_polars_parser("url")  # returns dict of parsed components
    parser_ref = make_polars_parser("ref")

    # Predicate pushdown
    lf_parsed = (
        lf.select(["id", "referrer", "url"])
        .with_columns(
            pl.col("url").map_elements(parser_url, return_dtype=url_struct_dtype("url")).alias("url_parsed"),
            pl.col("referrer").map_elements(parser_ref, return_dtype=url_struct_dtype("ref")).alias("ref_parsed"),
        )
        .unnest("url_parsed")
        .unnest("ref_parsed")
    )

    # Output path
    gold_parsed_root = gold_root / "parsed_url"
    out_dir = gold_parsed_root / f"event_date={event_date}"
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    out_path = out_dir / "part.parquet"

    # Stream/write to parquet
    lf_parsed.sink_parquet(str(out_path), compression=compression)

I need to increase processing speed so that backfilling daily histories takes hours, not days or weeks.

At this time, I've taken up a suggestion to build my own URL parsing engine in Rust (using the url and publicsuffix crates) for Python. I've been successful so far. The Rust program builds successfully and I am able to import the new library into python and run it. Results looks reasonable so far. I have a bit more pipeline work to do. I'll share the results when I'm done.

title: When and how should __all__ be defined?
body:
When should a module define __all__ vs using the underscore convention? Should this be done manually or dynamically?

Ideally, we could answer this once and for all with 'write it all out manually' and 'explicit is better than implicit', as has been said here. But in reality, cases such as these arise:

  • You are writing an __all__ for the __init__.py in the top level of a package, re-exporting perhaps hundreds of public functions and classes spread across multiple submodules. Now every edit to a nested file requires a trip to every __init__.py file, adding the new string to every __all__.
  • You are writing an __all__ for a constants.py storing hundreds of config constants. Now every insertion, deletion and modification of a constant has to happen to the __all__ too (two sources of truth).
  • You are defining parts of your API conditionally. For example, maybe a certain class is defined on Windows and not on Linux, or on Python >3.9 only. Or maybe a function is only defined under a try / except / else clause. Or maybe certain functionalities are only available for Pro users. That would require an __all__ += or __all__.append.

__all__ is supposed to solve:

  • Pollution of the global namespace (star imports)

  • Readable separation of public/private API

But when it is explicitly written out, you get:

  • Harder-to-maintain

  • Less DRY

But when it is dynamically generated (e.g. for-loop), you get:

  • Potentially unclear public API

  • Unhappy IDE/linter

Some other suggestions:

  • (as mentioned here) Prepend all unexported names - including modules, helpers, etc - with an underscore, and let the import machinery handle the rest. This is not something I do, because it would make the code less readable and me more annoyed (see the rejected PEP 842's Motivation).

  • Use the auto-all package as suggested here and here. However, this doesn't seem to be linter-friendly, and would be similar to using a dynamic list comprehension anyway.

  • Don't write __all__.

PEP 8 advises that 'modules should explicitly declare the names in their public API using the __all__ attribute'.

However, a github search in CPython yields:

__all__ = [x for x in dir(context._default_context) if not x.startswith('_')] # multiprocessing/__init__.py
__all__ = [name for name, obj in globals().items()
           if not name.startswith('_') and not isinstance(obj, types.ModuleType)
           and name not in {'wantobjects'}] # types.py
__all__.append("HTTPSConnection") # http/client.py
__all__.append('_exit') # os.py
__all__.append('SharedMemoryManager') # multiprocessing/managers.py

Writing __all__ dynamically is a common pattern.

title: Why does scikit-image skeletonization produce off-center loops and unwanted branches in thresholded handwritten strokes?
body:
I'm developing a handwriting-to-plotter application. I need to convert scanned handwritten text into one-pixel-wide centerlines and then trace those centerlines into coordinate polylines.

My problem is that the resulting skeletons are often significantly distorted: curves become jagged, some parts are not centered within the original strokes, and many short unwanted branches appear. This happens with several skeletonization algorithms, not just one.

What I have tried

I tested the following approaches:

  • Otsu and adaptive thresholding.

  • Sauvola thresholding using skimage.filters.threshold_sauvola.

  • Noise removal using remove_small_objects.

  • Morphological closing.

  • Morphological skeletonization using erosion and dilation.

  • Zhang–Suen thinning.

  • Guo–Hall thinning.

  • Lee thinning.

  • Medial axis extraction using skimage.morphology.medial_axis.

The results are still unsatisfactory. Changing the skeletonization algorithm does not consistently solve the distortion.

Current implementation

This is the preprocessing and skeletonization code I am currently testing:

from skimage import io, filters, morphology
from scipy.ndimage import distance_transform_edt
import numpy as np

img = io.imread("input.png", as_gray=True)

threshold = filters.threshold_sauvola(
    img,
    window_size=25,
    k=0.2
)

binary = img < threshold

binary = morphology.remove_small_objects(
    binary,
    min_size=64
)

binary = morphology.binary_closing(
    binary,
    morphology.disk(1)
)

skeleton = morphology.skeletonize(binary)

dist, medial = morphology.medial_axis(
    binary,
    return_distance=True
)

I have also tried converting the skeleton into a graph using sknw and networkx, then removing short leaf edges. However, this only addresses some unwanted branches; it does not fix the underlying geometric distortion.

Expected result

I want the skeleton to follow the center of the original handwriting strokes as accurately as possible.

The important requirements are:

  • Preserve the original shape of handwritten curves.

  • Avoid unnecessary branches and artifacts.

  • Preserve loops, intersections, and connections between strokes.

  • Produce continuous one-pixel-wide centerlines.

  • Avoid excessive smoothing that changes the handwriting geometry.

Error: The resulting skeleton contains geometric distortions. In particular, some loops are visibly off-center, and unwanted short branches appear along otherwise smooth strokes.

Is the problem caused by the binarized input, the skeletonization algorithm, or the geometry of the strokes themselves?

title: How to store objects in HTML5 localStorage/sessionStorage
body:
I'd like to store a JavaScript object in HTML5 localStorage, but my object is apparently being converted to a string.

I can store and retrieve primitive JavaScript types and arrays using localStorage, but objects don't seem to work. Should they?

Here's my code:

var testObject = { 'one': 1, 'two': 2, 'three': 3 };
console.log('typeof testObject: ' + typeof testObject);
console.log('testObject properties:');
for (var prop in testObject) {
    console.log('  ' + prop + ': ' + testObject[prop]);
}

// Put the object into storage
localStorage.setItem('testObject', testObject);

// Retrieve the object from storage
var retrievedObject = localStorage.getItem('testObject');

console.log('typeof retrievedObject: ' + typeof retrievedObject);
console.log('Value of retrievedObject: ' + retrievedObject);

The console output is

typeof testObject: object
testObject properties:
  one: 1
  two: 2
  three: 3
typeof retrievedObject: string
Value of retrievedObject: [object Object]

It looks to me like the setItem method is converting the input to a string before storing it.

I see this behavior in Safari, Chrome, and Firefox, so I assume it's my misunderstanding of the HTML5 Web Storage specification, not a browser-specific bug or limitation.

I've tried to make sense of the structured clone algorithm described in 2 Common infrastructure. I don't fully understand what it's saying, but maybe my problem has to do with my object's properties not being enumerable (???).

Is there an easy workaround?

Update: The W3C eventually changed their minds about the structured-clone specification, and decided to change the spec to match the implementations. See 12111 – spec for Storage object getItem(key) method does not match implementation behavior. So this question is no longer 100% valid, but the answers still may be of interest.

title: Why is conditional processing of a sorted array faster than of an unsorted array?
body:
In this C++ code, sorting the data (before the timed region) makes the primary loop ~6x faster:

#include <algorithm>
#include <ctime>
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    // Generate data
    const unsigned arraySize = 32768;
    int data[arraySize];

    for (unsigned c = 0; c < arraySize; ++c)
        data[c] = std::rand() % 256;

    // !!! With this, the next loop runs faster.
    std::sort(data, data + arraySize);

    // Test
    clock_t start = clock();
    long long sum = 0;
    for (unsigned i = 0; i < 100000; ++i)
    {
        for (unsigned c = 0; c < arraySize; ++c)
        {   // Primary loop.
            if (data[c] >= 128)
                sum += data[c];
        }
    }

    double elapsedTime = static_cast<double>(clock()-start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC;

    std::cout << elapsedTime << '\n';
    std::cout << "sum = " << sum << '\n';
}
  • Without std::sort(data, data + arraySize);, the code runs in 11.54 seconds.
  • With the sorted data, the code runs in 1.93 seconds.

(Sorting itself takes more time than this one pass over the array, so it's not actually worth doing if we needed to calculate this for an unknown array.)

Initially, I thought this might be just a language or compiler anomaly, so I tried Java:

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Random;

public class Main
{
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        // Generate data
        int arraySize = 32768;
        int data[] = new int[arraySize];

        Random rnd = new Random(0);
        for (int c = 0; c < arraySize; ++c)
            data[c] = rnd.nextInt() % 256;

        // !!! With this, the next loop runs faster
        Arrays.sort(data);

        // Test
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        long sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i)
        {
            for (int c = 0; c < arraySize; ++c)
            {   // Primary loop.
                if (data[c] >= 128)
                    sum += data[c];
            }
        }

        System.out.println((System.nanoTime() - start) / 1000000000.0);
        System.out.println("sum = " + sum);
    }
}

With a similar but less extreme result.

My first thought was that sorting brings the data into the cache, but that's silly because the array was just generated.

  • What is going on?
  • Why is processing a sorted array faster than processing an unsorted array?

The code is summing up some independent terms, so the order should not matter.

Related / follow-up Q&As with more modern C++ compilers

  • Why is processing an unsorted array the same speed as processing a sorted array with modern x86-64 clang? - modern C++ compilers auto-vectorize the loop, especially when SSE4.1 or AVX2 is available. This avoids any data-dependent branching so performance isn't data-dependent.
  • gcc optimization flag -O3 makes code slower than -O2 - branchless scalar with cmov can result in a longer dependency chain (especially when GCC chooses poorly), creating a latency bottleneck that makes it slower than branchy asm for the sorted case.

                      respObj = { error: `Error trying to subscribe ${req.body.email}. Please try again.`, message: response.body };
                    }
                    res.send(respObj);
                  } catch (err) {
                    var respErrorObj = { error: 'There was an error with your request', message: err.message };
                    res.send(respErrorObj);
                  }
            });
        })

        server.get('*', (req, res) => {
            return handle(req, res)
        })

        server.listen(3000, (err) => {
            if (err) throw err
            console.log('> Ready on http://localhost:3000')
        })
    })
    .catch((ex) => {
        console.error(ex.stack)
        process.exit(1)
    })

title: How does the JavaScript engine handle object identity and prototype inheritance between ShadowRealms and the main execution context?
body:
I’m experimenting with the ECMAScript proposal for ShadowRealm and ran into some deeply unintuitive behavior around object identity, function bindings, and prototype inheritance across realms.

Consider this example (run in an environment that supports ShadowRealm, like recent Chrome or Node.js with flags):

const realm = new ShadowRealm();

const fn = realm.evaluate(`
  globalThis.shared = { x: 1 };
  function getShared() { return shared; }
  getShared;
`);

const objFromRealm = fn();

console.log(objFromRealm); // [object Object]
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(objFromRealm) === Object.prototype); // false
console.log(objFromRealm instanceof Object); // false
console.log(typeof objFromRealm); // 'object'

Questions:

  • Why is the object returned from the ShadowRealm not an instance of Object in the main realm?

  • If realms are isolated, why does typeof objFromRealm still return 'object', even though it has a different prototype chain?

  • From the ECMAScript spec perspective: how is object identity and prototype linkage handled between different realms or compartments? Does the engine ever "wrap" or "proxy" objects to preserve memory safety?

  • Could this lead to identity leaks, instanceof inconsistencies, or cross-realm Function issues?

I tried accessing an object created inside a ShadowRealm from the main execution context. I expected it to behave like a normal object — for example, instanceof Object should return true, and the prototype should match the main realm’s Object.prototype. Instead, I found that objects from the ShadowRealm are not recognized as instances of Object in the main realm, and their prototype chains are completely separate. This behavior seems to break conventional expectations about object identity and typeof, so I’m trying to understand what’s really happening behind the scenes and whether this is by design or a side effect of compartment isolation.

title: Disabling content security policy of a Web page via a Chrome Extension
body:
I'm creating a Chrome Extension which modifies a script served by the server (which I have no control over) to add new functionality to the website, and I had the following idea:

  1. Block the original script via WebRequest, webRequestBlocking.
  2. Send the url of the blocked script to a script injected into the page.
  3. GET this url from the page's script.
  4. Edit a part of the code (string).
  5. Eval the string.

(Another working way is to redirect it to a local modified script return { redirectUrl: chrome.extension.getURL("modified.js") };, inside the Chrome Extension folder, but then it's impossible to modify it on the fly, that's why I want to eval a modified script)

When I try to eval the string in the 5th step, it says: ...'unsafe-eval' is not an allowed source of script in the following Content Security Policy directive: "script-src 'nonce-DFX4zDtBDF32343LjE2DFKMs' 'self' https://website.com".

I've tried to use webRequest.onHeadersReceived to see if I could alter CSP headers (as some answers suggested: Edit Content Security Policy in onHeadersReceived), but there is no "content-security-policy" header.

I can see a Content Security Policy meta tag (I've omitted everything except 'script-src'):

<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="script-src 'nonce-DFX4zDtBDF32343LjE2DFKMs' 'self' https://website.com; base-uri 'none';">

From this answer (https://stackoverflow.com/a/27324485/10364842), Chrome Extensions cannot override CSP of Web pages. But someone replies: I know this is incredibly old, but I came across it while trying to inject Artoo.js into a page. The chrome extension does indeed allow you to modify the page you're looking at and let any content through.

Eval works in the content script, but I need to execute the script in the page's context, because it depends on the global scope.

I'm wondering if it's possible to alter CSP of a Web page through a Chrome Extension, or if there is any other way to accomplish this solely via a Chrome extension?

title: How to implement CSP without 'unsafe-inline' in WordPress (Elementor) without breaking site?
body:
I am working on securing a WordPress website that uses Elementor and several plugins.

I have implemented a Content Security Policy (CSP) via .htaccess like this:

Header always set Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' https: data:; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://www.googletagmanager.com https://www.google-analytics.com; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https:; font-src 'self' https: data:; connect-src 'self' https:; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; frame-ancestors 'self';"

This works fine and the website functions correctly.

Problem:

Security tools (like Mozilla Observatory) report:

  • CSP implemented unsafely

  • Use of 'unsafe-inline' in script-src

  • Recommendation to remove 'unsafe-inline'

However, when I remove 'unsafe-inline':

  • Elementor layout breaks

  • Inline JavaScript stops working

  • Some features like search, forms, and UI interactions fail

  • Console shows CSP violations for inline scripts

What I Tried:

  1. Adding CSP nonce dynamically via PHP:

    • Injecting nonce into script tags

    • Using output buffering to modify <script> tags

  2. Restricting sources instead of using https:

  3. Allowing only required domains (Google Analytics, Tag Manager, etc.)

But Elementor and plugins still rely heavily on inline scripts, and removing 'unsafe-inline' breaks the site.

Question:

Is it possible to implement a strict CSP (without unsafe-inline) on a WordPress site using Elementor without breaking functionality?

If yes:

  • What is the recommended approach?

  • How to handle inline scripts generated by Elementor?

If not:

title: Can animation data of <AnimateMotion> (e.g. translation, rotation) be accessed via JavaScript in real-time?
body:
Assume the following example, directly taken from the W3 SVG 1.1 Standard Definition, section about <animateMotion>:

<?xml version="1.0" standalone="no"?>
<!DOCTYPE svg PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD SVG 1.1//EN" 
  "http://www.w3.org/Graphics/SVG/1.1/DTD/svg11.dtd">
<svg width="5cm" height="3cm"  viewBox="0 0 500 300"
     xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" version="1.1"
     xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" >
  <desc>Example animMotion01 - demonstrate motion animation computations</desc>
  <rect x="1" y="1" width="498" height="298"
        fill="none" stroke="blue" stroke-width="2" />
  <!-- Draw the outline of the motion path in blue, along
          with three small circles at the start, middle and end. -->
  <path id="path1" d="M100,250 C 100,50 400,50 400,250"
        fill="none" stroke="blue" stroke-width="7.06"  />
  <circle cx="100" cy="250" r="17.64" fill="blue"  />
  <circle cx="250" cy="100" r="17.64" fill="blue"  />
  <circle cx="400" cy="250" r="17.64" fill="blue"  />
  <!-- Here is a triangle which will be moved about the motion path.
       It is defined with an upright orientation with the base of
       the triangle centered horizontally just above the origin. -->
  <path d="M-25,-12.5 L25,-12.5 L 0,-87.5 z"
        fill="yellow" stroke="red" stroke-width="7.06"  >
    <!-- Define the motion path animation -->
    <animateMotion dur="6s" repeatCount="indefinite" rotate="auto" >
       <mpath xlink:href="#path1"/>
    </animateMotion>
  </path>
</svg>

This example showcases how a SVG element could be moved along a SVG path and keep always the correct orientation due to the rotate="auto" option. The screenshot of the W3 SVG Standard website shows the result.

The table explaining what is going on made me wonder:

Question

Is it possible to extract animation data (e.g. translation, rotation) from <animateMotion> via the JavaScript Web Animation API to modify additional parameters (e.g. the color of an SVG element according to the rotation angle)? Or is it similar to css based animations, where one has only very limited access (e.g. animation progress), but not to the current value of the animated property/properties? According to my research so far and my failed attempts, I would assume the latter.

title: How to safely generate unique Bitcoin receive addresses client-side in JavaScript?
body:
I'm trying to generate a unique receive address corresponding to a specific Bitcoin wallet of mine every time the visitor loads a static HTML page.

For security reasons, the server has no server-side dynamic scripting support (nor Bitcoin Core) and thus cannot "dispense" these from a database with pre-generated ones, or ask Bitcoin Core for one "live upon request".

The JavaScript library "bitcoinjs-lib" seems to be the only real choice.

Obviously I can't put the private key of the wallet (created with and managed by Bitcoin Core) on the server, let alone in a JavaScript that anyone can directly read. So it has to be "deterministic", or whatever the correct term is. The clever thing where you can create unlimited receive addresses based solely on some "public key" which is perfectly safe to have in public view.

I vaguely understand that I can ask Bitcoin Core once to generate "some kind of public key" for my wallet, then copy that string as a parameter to the webpage using bitcoinjs-lib, and it will then figure out a new unique address every time. But I'm not sure how this is done, and can't find out in spite of extensive searching and asking.

It seems like what I need is an "Extended Public Key (xpub)". Is that correct? And is the proper way to get that out from Bitcoin Core to make a `getdescriptorinfo` API call and then regexping out the right part of the "wpkh([d34db33f/84h/0h/0h]0279be667ef9dcbbac55a06295Ce870b07029Bfcdb2dce28d959f2815b16f81798)" return string (unsure which part), as "sort of" documented on https://bitcoincore.org/en/doc/30.0.0/rpc/util/getdescriptorinfo/ ?

But if so, I read this scary warning on https://github.com/bitcoinjs/bitcoinjs-lib :

Don't share BIP32 extended public keys ('xpubs'). They are a liability, and it only takes 1 misplaced private key (or a buggy implementation!) and you are vulnerable to catastrophic fund loss.

What do they mean by this? Don't share a public key? Isn't the whole point of a public key that it is meant to be posted in public, because it is not the private key? What do they mean by "it only takes 1 misplaced private key (or a buggy implementation!)"?

Are they perhaps specifically talking about some "old version" of these "xpubs"? Is BIP32 some deprecated/bad thing which has since been replaced? And if so, is whatever replaced it guaranteed to be safe to use?

I've been unable to find clear instructions of how exactly to be able to output with JavaScript a unique receive address for each page load, when bitcoinjs-lib is somehow fed only that "xpub" string. I'm not even 100% sure that it's possible, because it's always just implied or hinted at being the case.

I did find this interesting answer to a similar question: How to get bitcoin address from a public key with bitcoinjs

However, that code snippet is just made by "some dude" and doesn't really explain what it's doing, what that string represents or how they got it out from Bitcoin Core. Considering what is at stake, I'd rather not blindly trust this and "make assumptions", which has often in the past come back to bite me when I did assume that I had got it right, only to later realize that there had been some fundamental misunderstanding.

title: How can a user uninstall a Chrome JavaScript SpeechRecognition.install language pack?
body:
In Chrome you can now run the JavaScript command:

SpeechRecognition.install({
          langs: ["en-US"],
          processLocally: true,
        })

Any website can run it to install a language pack to run speech recognition locally. However as explained at https://issues.chromium.org/issues/521896368 , once you install a language pack then even if processLocally = false the Web Speech API will still use the local language pack if it is installed. There is no way for the user to know if it is using the cloud or local unless they disable their Internet. If speech recognition still works with Internet disabled then it is being processed locally. That presents a problem with users that want to go back to using the cloud because of poor performance from the local language pack because there are no instructions for uninstalling the language pack. There are no settings in Chrome. The closest setting that I can find in Chrome is "Live Caption". I found that if I turn on "Live Caption" and then remove the English language pack then the Web Speech API will start using the cloud again. But it is a very temporary fix. Within a few minutes it seems that Chrome automatically goes back to using the local language pack for SpeechRecognition. The SpeechRecognition.available will show that the language pack is back to "available" instead of "downloadable" and the Web Speech API will start being processed locally again.

So how can a user uninstall a SpeechRecognition language pack? It seems like a poor design to not let users easily see which language packs have been installed using SpeechRecognition.install along with no information about removing them.

title: Why is printing "B" dramatically slower than printing "#"?

 }

title: Fastest way to determine if an integer's square root is an integer
body:
I'm looking for the fastest way to determine if a long value is a perfect square (i.e. its square root is another integer):

  1. I've done it the easy way, by using the built-in Math.sqrt() function, but I'm wondering if there is a way to do it faster by restricting yourself to integer-only domain.
  2. Maintaining a lookup table is impractical (since there are about 231.5 integers whose square is less than 263).

Here is the very simple and straightforward way I'm doing it now:

public final static boolean isPerfectSquare(long n)
{
  if (n < 0)
    return false;

  long tst = (long)(Math.sqrt(n) + 0.5);
  return tst*tst == n;
}

Note: I'm using this function in many Project Euler problems. So no one else will ever have to maintain this code. And this kind of micro-optimization could actually make a difference, since part of the challenge is to do every algorithm in less than a minute, and this function will need to be called millions of times in some problems.

I've tried the different solutions to the problem:

  • After exhaustive testing, I found that adding 0.5 to the result of Math.sqrt() is not necessary, at least not on my machine.
  • The fast inverse square root was faster, but it gave incorrect results for n >= 410881. However, as suggested by BobbyShaftoe, we can use the FISR hack for n < 410881.
  • Newton's method was a good bit slower than Math.sqrt(). This is probably because Math.sqrt() uses something similar to Newton's Method, but implemented in the hardware so it's much faster than in Java. Also, Newton's Method still required use of doubles.
  • A modified Newton's method, which used a few tricks so that only integer math was involved, required some hacks to avoid overflow (I want this function to work with all positive 64-bit signed integers), and it was still slower than Math.sqrt().
  • Binary chop was even slower. This makes sense because the binary chop will on average require 16 passes to find the square root of a 64-bit number.
  • According to John's tests, using or statements is faster in C++ than using a switch, but in Java and C# there appears to be no difference between or and switch.
  • I also tried making a lookup table (as a private static array of 64 boolean values). Then instead of either switch or or statement, I would just say if(lookup[(int)(n&0x3F)]) { test } else return false;. To my surprise, this was (just slightly) slower. This is because array bounds are checked in Java.

title: Why is executing Java code in comments with certain Unicode characters allowed?
body:
The following code produces the output "Hello World!" (no really, try it).

public static void main(String... args) {

   // The comment below is not a typo.
   // \u000d System.out.println("Hello World!");
}

The reason for this is that the Java compiler parses the Unicode character \u000d as a new line and gets transformed into:

public static void main(String... args) {

   // The comment below is not a typo.
   //
   System.out.println("Hello World!");
}

Thus resulting into a comment being "executed".

Since this can be used to "hide" malicious code or whatever an evil programmer can conceive, why is it allowed in comments?

Why is this allowed by the Java specification?

Update:

In my original question, I used IntelliJ Idea. And like @dhke pointed out, IntelliJ got it wrong. However, I noticed that Idea 2024.1.1 addresses the issue directly. The formatting indicates that it is not a comment. Additionally, when auto-formatting, it will change \u000d to an actual new line. (I am not sure when this issue was addressed)

title: Which @NotNull Java annotation should I use?

  • javax.validation.constraints.NotNull

title: List.of()#iterator() exposes ListIterator interface but give UnsupportedOperationException when calling ListIterator methods
body:
This code does not work correctly

@Test(expected = UnsupportedOperationException.class)  
public void testListIteratorWrapperPreviousIndexThrows() {  
  List<String> immutable = List.of("a", "b", "c");  
  Iterator<String> it = immutable.iterator();
  ListIteratorWrapper w = new ListIteratorWrapper<>(it);
  w.next(); // works
  w.previousIndex(); // throws UOE
}

and this is why

import java.util.*;

public class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    var l = List.of(1,2,3);
    var itr = l.iterator();
    //  This instaceof is true!
    if(itr instanceof ListIterator li)  {
      System.out.println("itr is a ListIterator! O.o");
      //  call to .nextIndex() should return 0
      //  but throws UOE
     System.out.println(li.nextIndex());
    }
  }
}

Stacktrace is

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException
        at java.base/java.util.ImmutableCollections.uoe(ImmutableCollections.java:159)
        at java.base/java.util.ImmutableCollections$ListItr.nextIndex(ImmutableCollections.java:432)
        at Main.main(Main.java:16)

The problem is that Iterator it should be a simple Iterator and should not be detected as a ListIterator; the “problem” is in JDK class java.util.ImmutableCollections.AbstractImmutableList<E> and java.util.ImmutableCollections.ListItr<E>: #iterator() return a inner ListItr which acts as an Iterator or a ListIterator but implements ListIterator interface.
ListIteratorWrapper use instanceof to check if delegated iterator is a ListIterator: wrapped iterator returns true but acts as a simple Iterator.
Is this a well-known problem or should be reported?

title: High level design for messenger like whats app?
body:
I need to design the similar stuff like whats app or any messenger like module.

High level flow

Client > Load Balancer > Web servers(assume 10 clustered server for now) > Rest based controller > Service > DAO > DB

Challenge :-

say Friend 1 and Friend 2 are online . Friend 1 has established HTTP web connection to web server 1 and Friend 2 has established HTTP web connection to web server 2. Friend 1 send the message to Friend 2.

Now as soon as message comes to web server 1, i need to convey the message to web server 2 so that message can be pushed back to friend 2 through already established web connection

I have couple of related questions here :-

  1. I can use distributed queues to propagate the message from one server to another. As soon as message comes to one server , it will push it to distributed queue(distribute queue because of load balancing and high availability) with message content, fromUserId, toUserId. My question how the right server (in this case web server 2) will be notified ? because if i use JMS queue , only one server will be notified through listener. If i use topic all servers will be notified . In this case all servers can reject the message except the one server where fromUserId resides. Is there a better way where queue just notifies the right server based on some meta data ?

Also if destinationUserId is offline, i need to put back the message on queue. Not sure how it can be achieved ? I believe we need to use some other queue implementation(probably java based in-memory queue) instead of JMS queue/topic ? Server code will only remove the message from custom queue once it gets acknowledgement from client.

  1. If any client is offline at the time message is sent, in that case whe he coming online,he will send the pull request . Server will make the request to distributed queue , distributed queue will pull the message from right physical queue. My question ia should distributed queue will keep the destinationUserId and message as value in metadata ?

  2. DB vs Queue :- With this approach i believe there is no need to store the message in DB which can be costly(time complexity) than queue(in-memory queue) in highly real time application like messenger. We just need to store user/group details in db.

Update :- I found related link at quora where last point i.e. What protocol is used in Whatsapp app ?... by Kah Seng Tay also confirms the simialr approach using queue , but still my above questions on queue are yet to be answered.

title: Cannot call Connection.commit in distributed transaction
body:
I am using Weblogic 12c and I am getting the below error while committing distributed transactions in my application.

"java.sql.SQLException: Cannot call Connection.commit in distributed transaction. Transaction Manager will commit the resource manager when the distributed transaction is committed"

The part of code throwing exception is:

Session sessionNew = HibernateService.getService().getSession();
sessionNew.connection().commit();

This question has been asked several times, but the solution I am seeking is different. The most common solution is to disable XA transactions to resolve the issue. But my application contains more than resources like database, JMS etc. Can anyone please suggest a solution other than the one mentioned above.

Also, I needed to understand if there is any relation between JTA transaction timeout value and the above-mentioned error.

Thanks a lot.

title: Java Timer Swing Exactly 60 fps
body:
I have an animation in a JPanel that updates itself through a javax.swing.Timer. This timer can be constructed to have a delay in milliseconds that must be an integer. If I were to have the JPanel update 60 times each second, I would set the delay to 1000/60 = ~16.6666. However, this delay must be an int, so I have the option of rounding up or down. For a delay of 16 milliseconds, the animation would update at 62.5 frames per second. Rounding up to 17 millisecond delay would give a frame rate of 58.824.

How would I go about having a frame rate of exactly 60 frames per second?

Thanks in advance.

title: Code Coverage for Cucumber Tests using Jacoco
body:
I am trying to integrate Jacoco to get the code coverage for my Cucumber tests using Maven. Following is my project structure:

  • -src-main-java-Pages

  • -src-main-java-Helper

  • -src-test-java-resources-features

  • -src-test-java-Steps

Following is the Jacoco configuration in my POM.xml

          <plugin>
            <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
            <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            <version>0.8.2</version>
            <configuration>
                <destFile>${basedir}/target/coverage-reports/jacoco.exec</destFile>
                <dataFile>${basedir}/target/coverage-reports/jacoco.exec</dataFile>
                <outputDirectory>${basedir}/target/coverage-reports/jacoco</outputDirectory>
            </configuration>
            <executions>
                <execution>
                    <id>prepare-agent</id>
                    <goals>
                        <goal>prepare-agent</goal>
                    </goals>
                </execution>
                <execution>
                    <id>report</id>
                    <goals>
                        <goal>report</goal>
                    </goals>
                </execution>
                <execution>
                    <id>check</id>
                    <goals>
                        <goal>check</goal>
                    </goals>
                    <configuration>
                        <rules>
                            <rule>
                                <element>PACKAGE</element>
                                <includes>
                                    <include>**/*Steps.*</include>
                                </includes>
                            </rule>
                            <rule>
                                <element>PACKAGE</element>
                                <excludes>
                                    <exclude>**/*Pages.*</exclude>
                                    <exclude>**/*Page.*</exclude>
                                </excludes>
                            </rule>
                        </rules>
                    </configuration>
                </execution>
            </executions>
        </plugin>

I am able to generate the code coverage report. However, in the report, it covers all the classes in the -src-main packages. As per different google researches and SO posts, I tried to modify my POM to exclude Pages and include only Steps in my code coverage report. But somehow, it keeps on displaying all the files in the main package.

Am I taking the wrong approach? I just want to create a report which does code coverage for only the tests that I execute rather than all the files in the main package.

body:
I am currently new in grpc. I wanted to provide ssl for my grpc server the javav code for starting looks like this:

title: NewRelic: Ignore Spring Boot Actuator Transactions
body:
We've got NewRelic integrated into Spring Boot. I don't know why but since yesterday NR identifies all requests to actuator endpoints (including the health check and prometheus endpoints that get polled very frequently) as web transactions and tracks them accordingly.

The additional traffic is adding a serious traffic overhead to some of our internal systems that are not web facing. This means that problems become harder to see (all the health check requests are super quick and successful, so the error rates of the application become much lower and therefore harder to notice. also response times and APEX score are now looking super good but are in fact meaningless.

I've tried to disable NR for the /actuator endpoint in various ways, but I seem to be unable to do so. I've tried to add a custom instrumentation to ignore the transaction (via XML upload and in the UI) but this does not help. Other than this, the only way to ignore the transaction is via code, but as actuator is part of the spring framework I am not able to modify its code.

Do you have any suggestions on how to make NR ignore the actuator endpoint that actually works?

title: Why does Java suggest List<? extends Class<?>> instead of List<Class<?>>?
body:
I'm working with a record that stores a class and its annotations:

record ClassMetaData(Class<?> clazz, List<Annotation> annotationList) {}

I have a method that filters classes based on an annotation:

public List<Class<?>> getClassesByPresentAnnotation(
        Class<? extends Annotation> annotation) {

    Function<ClassMetaData, Class<?>> f =
            metadata -> metadata.clazz();

    return annotationMetadataByClass.stream()
            .map(e -> f.apply(e))
            .filter(clazz -> clazz.isAnnotationPresent(annotation))
            .toList();
}

The code doesn't compile, and my IDE suggests changing the return type to List<? extends Class<?>>.

I don't really understand why I need ? extends here.

My record's clazz() returns Class<?>, and my Function also explicitly returns Class<?>.

So why isn't List<Class<?>> enough? What's the difference between these two return types in this case?

annotationMetadataByClass is declared as List of ClassMetaData.

Here's the exact compiler error:

java: incompatible types:
java.util.List<java.lang.Class<capture#1 of ?>>
cannot be converted to java.util.List<java.lang.Class<?>>

The IDE's suggested fix works, but I'm more interested in understanding what's actually happening here and how Java's type inference works in this case.

title: An inspection cursor remains readable after its JDBC Statement is closed
body:
An inspection-page cursor should be closed when its owning statement is disposed. With Apache IoTDB 2.0.10, JDBC driver 2.0.10, table dialect, and Java 17.0.9, I can still advance the cursor after closing that statement.

The inspection samples are:

CREATE DATABASE inspection_preview;
USE inspection_preview;
CREATE TABLE checks(station STRING TAG,score INT32 FIELD);
INSERT INTO checks(time,station,score) VALUES (1000,'north',10),(2000,'north',20),(3000,'north',30);

The query itself reads these three scores:

SELECT score FROM checks ORDER BY time;

+-----+
|score|
+-----+
|   10|
|   20|
|   30|
+-----+

Save this as InspectionCursor.java. Set IOTDB_JDBC_URL to a table-dialect connection URL (?sql_dialect=table), and supply IOTDB_USER and IOTDB_PASSWORD in the environment. With the 2.0.10 distribution libraries in lib, run:

java -cp "lib/*" InspectionCursor.java

import java.sql.*;

public class InspectionCursor {
  public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
    Class.forName("org.apache.iotdb.jdbc.IoTDBDriver");
    try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(
        System.getenv("IOTDB_JDBC_URL"),
        System.getenv("IOTDB_USER"),
        System.getenv("IOTDB_PASSWORD"))) {
      System.out.println("JDBC driver=" + c.getMetaData().getDriverVersion());
      Statement s = c.createStatement();
      ResultSet r = null;
      try {
        s.execute("USE inspection_preview");
        r = s.executeQuery("SELECT score FROM checks ORDER BY time");
        r.next();
        System.out.println("before close: statement=" + s.isClosed()
            + ", resultSet=" + r.isClosed());
        s.close();
        System.out.println("after Statement.close: statement=" + s.isClosed()
            + ", resultSet=" + r.isClosed());
        try {
          boolean advanced = r.next();
          System.out.println("next after Statement.close=" + advanced);
          if (advanced) System.out.println("score after close=" + r.getInt("score"));
        } catch (SQLException e) {
          System.out.println("next after Statement.close -> " + e.getClass().getName());
        }
        r.close();
        System.out.println("after ResultSet.close: resultSet=" + r.isClosed());
      } finally {
        if (r != null) r.close();
        s.close();
      }
    }
  }
}

The program prints:

JDBC driver=2.0.10
before close: statement=false, resultSet=false
after Statement.close: statement=true, resultSet=false
next after Statement.close=true
score after close=20
after ResultSet.close: resultSet=true

The owning statement reports isClosed() == true, but the current result set reports false and yields score 20 on its next call. Calling ResultSet.close() directly then changes the result-set state to true.

I expected the current result set to be closed automatically: the JDBC Statement.close() contract says that closing a statement also closes its current result set.

Why does closing this statement leave its current result set usable in the 2.0.10 driver?

        setDataSource(dataSource);
        setFunction(true);
        setSql(functionName);

        if(getOutput() == null && getMapper() != null) {
            super.declareParameter(new SqlOutParameter("cursor", OracleTypes.CURSOR, getMapper()));
        }
        else {
            super.declareParameter(new SqlOutParameter("cursor", OracleTypes.CURSOR, new BeanPropertyRowMapper(getOutput())));
        }

        for (Map.Entry<String,Object> entry : inputs.entrySet()) {
            Object value = inputs.get(entry.getKey());
            LOGGER.debug("Parametro {} ",entry.getKey());
            LOGGER.debug("Valor {} ",value);
            super.declareParameter(new SqlParameter(entry.getKey(), OracleStoreProcedure.getType(value)));
        }

        compile();
        String fn = functionName+"("+inputs+")";

        //LOGGER.info(fn);
        try {
            Map resultado = super.execute(inputs);
            return (List) resultado.get("cursor");
        }
        catch(Throwable seq){
            logger.info("Ocurrio un problema al invocar la funcion{}", seq);
            return new ArrayList();
        }
    }
}

body:
This is my first time posting to this blog. I'm new to Java and I have an issue with using bubble sort when a user inputs a set of values. Below is my code; however, I'm looking more for advice then an answer because I won't learn the language with the answer.

Thanks for your help and again sorry if my code is a little convoluted. BTW, I just started to learn Java so I won't be able to follow very complex coding advice.

import java.util.Arrays;
public class bubbleSort{

    public static void main(String[] arg){

        java.util.Scanner input = new java.util.Scanner(System.in);
        System.out.println("Enter total amount of numbers:" );

        int n = input.nextInt();

        int [] numbers = new int[n];

        System.out.println("Enter the numbers: ");
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
           numbers[i] = input.nextInt();
        }

        System.out.println(list(n));

        bubbleSort(n);

        System.out.println(list(n));    
    }


    public static void bubbleSort(int[] n){

        boolean flag;

        do{

            flag = false; 

            for(int i = 0; i < n.length - 1; i++){

                if (n[i] > n[i + 1]){

                    int temp = n[i];
                    n[i] = n[i + 1];
                    n[i + 1] = temp;

                    flag = true;
                }

            }

        } while (flag);
    }
 }

title: Speed improvement of highlighting matching term in filterable JComboBox
body:
I made custom class for filterable JComboBox. I tried with 10000 items and it works pretty well (nothing is laggy) although I won't even need that much items for my usecase. Then I tried implementing highlighting of a matching term. Idea is to match string that I'm typing in textfield to part of item and to highlight that matching part. I implemented it and it works but the problem is that it is laggy (takes a lot of time to open popup and to highlight items) when combobox has apx. 1000 items and more. How can I improve speed so that it is not laggy?

FilterableComboBox

import javax.swing.*;
import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.KeyAdapter;
import java.awt.event.KeyEvent;
import java.util.ArrayList;

public class FilterableJComboBox extends JComboBox<String> {

    private final ArrayList<String> items;

    public FilterableJComboBox(java.util.List<String> items, boolean shouldHighlight) {
        super(items.toArray(new String[0]));
        this.items = new ArrayList<>(items);

        setEditable(true);

        JTextField textField = (JTextField) getEditor().getEditorComponent();

        if (shouldHighlight)
            turnOnHighlight(textField);

        textField.addKeyListener(new KeyAdapter() {
            @Override
            public void keyReleased(KeyEvent e) {

                if (e.getKeyCode() == KeyEvent.VK_UP ||
                    e.getKeyCode() == KeyEvent.VK_DOWN ||
                    e.getKeyCode() == KeyEvent.VK_LEFT ||
                    e.getKeyCode() == KeyEvent.VK_RIGHT ||
                    e.getKeyCode() == KeyEvent.VK_ESCAPE ||
                    e.isControlDown()) {
                    return;
                }

                if (e.getKeyCode() == KeyEvent.VK_ENTER && getModel().getSize() == 1) {
                    setSelectedIndex(0);
                    textField.setText(getModel().getSelectedItem().toString());
                    textField.setCaretPosition(textField.getText().length());
                    return;
                }

                if (e.getKeyCode() == KeyEvent.VK_ENTER)
                    return;

                int caretPos = textField.getCaretPosition();
                int selectionStart = textField.getSelectionStart();
                int selectionEnd = textField.getSelectionEnd();

                String text = textField.getText();
                String lowerCaseText = text.toLowerCase();

                DefaultComboBoxModel<String> model = new DefaultComboBoxModel<>();
                for (String item : FilterableJComboBox.this.items)
                    if (item.toLowerCase().contains(lowerCaseText))
                        model.addElement(item);

                setModel(model);

                textField.setText(text);
                textField.setCaretPosition(Math.min(textField.getText().length(), caretPos));
                textField.setSelectionStart(Math.min(textField.getText().length(), selectionStart));
                textField.setSelectionEnd(Math.min(textField.getText().length(), selectionEnd));

                setPopupVisible(model.getSize() > 0);
            }
        });
    }

    public void turnOnHighlight(JTextField textField) {
        setRenderer(new DefaultListCellRenderer() {
            @Override
            public Component getListCellRendererComponent(JList<?> list, Object value, int index, boolean isSelected, boolean cellHasFocus) {
                JLabel label = (JLabel) super.getListCellRendererComponent(list, value, index, isSelected, cellHasFocus);

                if (value != null) {
                    String itemText = value.toString();
                    String searchText = textField.getText();

                    if (index < 0 || !isPopupVisible() || searchText.isEmpty()) {
                        label.setText(itemText);
                        return label;
                    }

                    int startIdx = itemText.toLowerCase().indexOf(searchText.toLowerCase());
                    if (startIdx != -1) {
                        int endIdx = startIdx + searchText.length();

                        String before = itemText.substring(0, startIdx);
                        String match = itemText.substring(startIdx, endIdx);
                        String after = itemText.substring(endIdx);

                        label.setText("<html>" + before + "<span style='background: #ede740; color: black;'>" + match + "</span>" + after + "</html>");
                    } else {
                        label.setText(itemText);
                    }
                }
                return label;
            }
        });
    }

    public boolean isInOriginalItems(String value) {
        return this.items.stream().anyMatch(item -> item.equalsIgnoreCase(value));
    }
}
