title: Best practices for DTO mapping in jOOQ 3.20 + Kotlin Spring boot Web Apps
body:
I recently started using jOOQ, and I absolutely love it. I really appreciate how intuitive it is writing jOOQ code feels exactly like writing raw MySQL.

However, as a beginner, I'm struggling to find the "recommended" architecture for my specific use case, and I'd love to get some advice from experienced users.

My tech stack:

  • Kotlin + Spring Boot
  • MySQL 8+
  • jOOQ 3.20.10

Context and problem

I am building a web application specifically an admin dashboard, not just a simple REST API. Because of this, my screens require complex data grids fetching data from multiple joined tables. To optimize I/O, I don't fetch entire tables; instead, I use a large number of specific, read-only DTOs containing only the necessary fields.

At first, I took the simple approach: fetching records and mapping them directly using record.into(MyDto::class.java). However, I quickly ran into the "name fallback/collision" issue. Since into() maps by column name using reflection as fallback, joining tables with identical column names (e.g., id, status, type created_at) caused jOOQ to inject the wrong values into my DTOs.

The dilemma: this made me realize that my DTO design and mapping strategy need a complete overhaul.

  • Using into(POJO) is too risky for complex joins due to name collisions.

  • Using explicit record.get(TABLE.FIELD) for exact matching is safe, but it requires a massive amount of boilerplate code for dozens of DTOs.

  • Using row mapping requires exact orderings in DTO fields, which might be fragile to human errors.

Example code

I made a static fields array inside the DTO's companion object to centralize the projection definition. My goal was to easily pass these fields into the SELECT clause without repeating myself, keeping the exact column references tied to the DTO.

Here is a simplified example of my pojo mapping setup:

// 1. DTO Definition
data class ArticleDto(
    val articleId: Long? = null,
    val authorId: Long?,
    val title: String?,
    val viewCount: Int?,
    val isPublished: Boolean?
) {
    companion object {
        val fields = arrayOf(
            ARTICLE.ID.`as`("articleId"),
            ARTICLE.AUTHOR_ID.`as`("authorId"),
            ARTICLE.TITLE,
            ARTICLE.VIEW_COUNT,
            ARTICLE.IS_PUBLISHED
        )
    }
}

// 2. Repository Usage
fun getPublishedArticles(): List<ArticleDto> {
    return dslContext
        .select(*ArticleDto.fields, OtherDto.fields...) 
        .from(ARTICLE)
        .leftJoin(USER).on(ARTICLE.AUTHOR_ID.eq(USER.ID))
        .leftJoin() ... 
        .where(ARTICLE.IS_PUBLISHED.eq(true))
        .fetch { record ->
            // ⚠️ BUT here is where the pain begins...
            
            // Approach A: Manual exact match (Safe, but too much boilerplate)
            /*
            ArticleDto(
                articleId = record.get(ARTICLE.ID.`as`("articleId")),
                title = record.get(ARTICLE.TITLE),
                // ... repetitive ...
            )
            */

            // Approach B: Using into() (Short, but risks name collisions like USER.ID vs ARTICLE.ID)
            /*
            record.into(ArticleDto::class.java)
            */
        }
}

For example, this heavily joined data are all related to the main data A, which I would like to fetch them in one nested DTO. But as more tables get joined, risk of mapping problems rise.

So, after realizing the name collision issues with the simple POJO mapping (into()), I started looking for a better direction and found out about jOOQ's row() mapping feature.

I tried applying it to my DTOs, and it seemed like the perfect solution at first. However, despite its type-safety, I quickly realized that it still comes with critical limitations: the mapping relies strictly on the positional order of the fields (which is fragile), and it is hard-bound by the 22-arity limit (Row22)."

data class OrderShippingExtra(
    val vendorCode: String?,
    val destZoneName: String?,
    val destAddress: String?,
    val status: String?
) {
    companion object {
        // Allows overriding fields for aliased tables
        fun row(
            destZoneNameField: Field<String?>, // Mandatory override example
            vendorCodeField: Field<String?> = VENDOR.CODE
        ) = DSL.row(
            vendorCodeField,
            destZoneNameField,
            ORDER.DEST_ADDRESS,
            ORDER.STATUS
        ).mapping { vendorCode, destZoneName, destAddress, status ->
            // ⚠️ Issue 1: Strict Positional Fragility here!
            OrderShippingExtra(
                vendorCode = vendorCode,
                destZoneName = destZoneName,
                destAddress = destAddress,
                status = status
            )
        }
    }
}


fun getOrderDetailData(orderId: Long): OrderDetailData? {
    val destZone = ZONE.`as`("destZone")

    return dsl.select(
        OrderCore.row(),
        OrderShippingExtra.row(destZoneNameField = destZone.NAME), // Passing aliased field
        // ... ⚠️ Issue 2: If we add more rows/fields here, we hit the Row22 limit!
    )
    .from(ORDER)
    .leftJoin(VENDOR).on(ORDER.VENDOR_ID.eq(VENDOR.ID))
    .leftJoin(destZone).on(ORDER.DEST_ZONE_ID.eq(destZone.ID))
    .where(ORDER.ID.eq(orderId))
    .fetchOne(Records.mapping(::OrderDetailData))
}

Last example is what i am trying to adopt. Instead of using row().mapping, the DTO retains a fields array, and row().convertFrom is applied directly in the select clause.

This allows grouping of the result set for each DTO, minimizing mapping issues caused by name collisions or positional fragility.

data class ReceiptDto(
    val id: Long?,
    val baseAmount: Int?,
    val timeAmount: Int?
) {
    companion object {
        val fields = arrayOf(
            RECEIPT.ID,
            RECEIPT.BASE_AMOUNT,
            RECEIPT.TIME_AMOUNT
        )
    }
}

fun getOrderSummaries(): List<OrderSummaryData> {
    val receiptField = DSL.field(
        row(*ReceiptDto.fields)
            .convertFrom { it.into(ReceiptDto::class.java) }
    )

    return dsl.select(*OrderSummaryDto.fields, receiptField)
        .from(ORDERS)
        .leftJoin(RECEIPT).on(ORDERS.ID.eq(RECEIPT.ORDER_ID))
        .fetch { r ->
            OrderSummaryData(
                summary = r.into(OrderSummaryDto::class.java),
                receipt = r.get(receiptField)
            )
        }
}

My Questions:

  1. In a heavily joined, read-heavy web application like this, how do you recommend separating and structuring DTOs for better use of Jooq queries?

  2. What is the best practice for mapping a Record to a Kotlin data class safely (avoiding name clashes) without drowning in manual mapping boilerplate?

  3. Since I am on jOOQ 3.20, should I be leaning heavily into ROW and MULTISET for structural mapping right at the SQL level, or do you prefer keeping the SQL flat and handling the mapping via Kotlin extension functions/external mappers?

I know that this might be a broader architectural or structural design issue rather than just a simple "how to use a jOOQ API" question. However, since my goal is to solve this data access layer entirely within the jOOQ ecosystem, I am hoping to tap into the insights of veterans who have gone through this exact trial and error.

Any insights on how you architect your DTOs and mapping layers in production would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks!

We are facing an intermittent issue with Spring Kafka where a consumer stops processing messages after some time. Restarting the application fixes the issue temporarily for some topics.

Environment

  • Spring Boot

  • Spring Kafka

  • @KafkaListener

  • AckMode.MANUAL_IMMEDIATE

  • FixedBackOff

title: Spring Boot endpoint that returns 202 with a jobId and runs a long sync task in the background
body:
I'm working on a university project for a water billing office. The office has a legacy system with a MySQL database that we are not allowed to modify. As part of a new feature, we created a separate Spring Boot service that reads from that database with a read-only user and copies the new or changed records (customers, water consumption and payments) to Amazon DynamoDB, so that other services can query them without touching the legacy system.

The sync can take several minutes, so the API contract we agreed on says that the client should not wait for it to finish. The client calls the generate endpoint with a POST request, the service immediately answers with HTTP 202 Accepted and a job ID, and later the client calls the jobs endpoint with that ID to check if the job is pending, running, completed or failed.

In my first version, the controller generates a random ID for the job, saves its status in an in-memory map, starts the sync in a new thread and immediately returns the 202 response with the job ID. When the thread finishes, it updates the map to completed, or to failed if an exception is thrown.

This works in my local tests, but I noticed two problems that I don't know how to solve properly.

First, if the container restarts, the map is lost, so asking for the status of a job that actually ran returns 404.

Second, if someone calls the generate endpoint several times quickly, several syncs run at the same time and write the same records to DynamoDB in parallel.

Is it better to use the Async annotation with a ThreadPoolTaskExecutor and store the job status in a database table instead of in memory? And what is the recommended way in Spring Boot to make sure only one sync job runs at a time?

  config:

  config:
    import: vault://secret-dev/application-dev

  • application-prod.yml:

  config:
    import: vault://secret-prod/application-prod

When I start the application with the prod profile active: java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

I expect Spring Boot to use the Vault path defined in application-prod.yml (secret-prod/application-prod) instead of the default path defined in application.yml (secret-dev/application-dev).

However, both imports appear to be processed. How does Spring Boot 2.7 handle list merging for spring.config.import across profile-specific files, and what is the recommended way to make profile-specific Vault imports mutually exclusive?

title: JPA save inside rabbitmq listener
body:
I am trying to save an entity consumed inside a queue using rabbit mq. I have encountered

some problems.

First of all : The consumed event will give me an entity which already has an id. My user entity has an automatic generation ID annotation on UUID id attribute. How should I approach this? For example I know I could implement Persistable interface, but won't this have compatibility issues with the already implemented methods which depend on that automatic id generation?

Second: How do you check correctly if the toPersist entity was actually saved in db ? I used a try catch but I found out I should use a saveAndFlush() because save() will not throw exception immediately. It will throw exception only when the insert is tried and that can be after the try catch executed.

Third: should I check that the consumed entity doesn't have any null fields ( id) since the publisher checks that already before sending ?

Here is the code :

 @RabbitListener(queues = "user.created")
@Transactional
public void createUser(MessageEnvelope<UserRegistrationEvent> envelope) {
    UserRegistrationEvent event = envelope.payload();
    User toPersist = userMapper.toUserFromPayload(event);

    if (userRepository.existsById(toPersist.getId())) {
        logger.warn("User with id {} already exists", toPersist.getId());
        return;
    }
    try {
        User managedUser = userRepository.saveAndFlush(toPersist);
    }catch(Exception e){
        rabbitMQProducer.publishRegistrationFailed(toPersist);
    }
}

title: Angular/RxJS When should I unsubscribe from `Subscription`
body:
When should I store the Subscription instances and invoke unsubscribe() during the ngOnDestroy life cycle and when can I simply ignore them?

Saving all subscriptions introduces a lot of mess into component code.

HTTP Client Guide ignore subscriptions like this:

getHeroes() {
  this.heroService.getHeroes()
                  .subscribe(
                     heroes => this.heroes = heroes,
                     error =>  this.errorMessage = <any>error);
}

In the same time Route & Navigation Guide says that:

Eventually, we'll navigate somewhere else. The router will remove this component from the DOM and destroy it. We need to clean up after ourselves before that happens. Specifically, we must unsubscribe before Angular destroys the component. Failure to do so could create a memory leak.

We unsubscribe from our Observable in the ngOnDestroy method.

private sub: any;

ngOnInit() {
  this.sub = this.route.params.subscribe(params => {
     let id = +params['id']; // (+) converts string 'id' to a number
     this.service.getHero(id).then(hero => this.hero = hero);
   });
}

ngOnDestroy() {
  this.sub.unsubscribe();
}

title: *ngIf and *ngFor on same element causing error
body:
I'm having a problem with trying to use Angular's *ngFor and *ngIf on the same element.

When trying to loop through the collection in the *ngFor, the collection is seen as null and consequently fails when trying to access its properties in the template.

@Component({
  selector: 'shell',
  template: `
    <h3>Shell</h3><button (click)="toggle()">Toggle!</button>

    <div *ngIf="show" *ngFor="let thing of stuff">
      {{log(thing)}}
      <span>{{thing.name}}</span>
    </div>
  `
})

export class ShellComponent implements OnInit {

  public stuff:any[] = [];
  public show:boolean = false;

  constructor() {}

  ngOnInit() {
    this.stuff = [
      { name: 'abc', id: 1 },
      { name: 'huo', id: 2 },
      { name: 'bar', id: 3 },
      { name: 'foo', id: 4 },
      { name: 'thing', id: 5 },
      { name: 'other', id: 6 },
    ]
  }

  toggle() {
    this.show = !this.show;
  }

  log(thing) {
    console.log(thing);
  }

}

I know the easy solution is to move the *ngIf up a level but for scenarios like looping over list items in a ul, I'd end up with either an empty li if the collection is empty, or my lis wrapped in redundant container elements.

Example at this plnkr.

Note the console error:

EXCEPTION: TypeError: Cannot read property 'name' of null in [{{thing.name}} in ShellComponent@5:12]

Am I doing something wrong or is this a bug?

                StompHeaderAccessor accessor = MessageHeaderAccessor.getAccessor(message, StompHeaderAccessor.class);

                log.info("in override " + accessor.getCommand());

                    if (Objects.nonNull(authentication))

                    else

            @Override

                StompHeaderAccessor sha = StompHeaderAccessor.wrap(message);

                if (sha.getCommand() == null) {
                    log.warn("postSend null command");
                    return;
                }

                String sessionId = sha.getSessionId();

                switch (sha.getCommand()) {
                    case CONNECT:

                        break;
                    case CONNECTED:

                    case DISCONNECT:

title: How to access current attempt count in Spring Boot 4's native for soft vs hard retry limits?
body:
With the native retry support in Spring Boot 4 / Spring Framework, org.springframework.core.retry.RetryPolicy uses a simplified method signature:

public interface RetryPolicy {
    boolean shouldRetry(Throwable throwable);
}

Unlike legacy Spring Retry which passed a RetryContext (canRetry(RetryContext)), the new native shouldRetry method only accepts a Throwable.

Our Use Case

We need to implement a dynamic retry strategy with two distinct tiers of retry limits:

  • Soft Retries (maxSoftRetries): Used when the cause is an instance of SoftRetryableException.

  • Default Retries (maxRetries): Used for all other retryable exceptions.

The Problem

Because shouldRetry(Throwable) only receives the Throwable instance without an execution context, we are unsure how to cleanly access the current attempt count at runtime to compare it against maxSoftRetries vs currentFailures.

Here is a simplified version of what we are trying to achieve:

public class TieredRetryPolicy implements RetryPolicy {

    private static final ThreadLocal<Integer> softFailureCount = ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> 0);

    private final RetryPolicy delegate;
    private final int maxSoftAttempts;

public TieredRetryPolicy(BackOff backOff, int maxSoftAttempts) {
    this.maxSoftAttempts = maxSoftAttempts;
    this.delegate = RetryPolicy.builder()
                .backOff(backOff)
                .includes(SoftRetriableException.class, RetriableException.class)
                .excludes(NonRetriableException.class)
                .build();
}

@Override
public boolean shouldRetry(Throwable throwable) {
    if (throwable == null) {
            softFailureCount.remove();
            return true;
        }
    Throwable cause = resolveMessageExceptionCause(throwable);
    if (cause instanceof SoftRetriableException) {
// How do we obtain the current attempt count in a thread-safe manner here instead of ThreadLocal?
          int failures = softFailureCount.get() + 1;
          softFailureCount.set(failures);
          return failures < maxSoftAttempts;
     }
     return delegate.shouldRetry(throwable);
  }
}

@Bean
public RetryPolicy chroniclerRetryPolicy() {
    ExponentialBackOff backOff = new ExponentialBackOff();
    backOff.setInitialInterval(props.getInitialInterval());
    backOff.setMaxInterval(props.getMaxInterval());
    backOff.setMultiplier(props.getMultiplier());
    backOff.setMaxAttempts(props.getMaxAttemptsForBackOff());

    return new ChroniclerRetryPolicy(backOff,rops.getMaxSoftAttempts());
}

We have custom RetryListener from core.retry but it still doesn't help us with it.

RetryListener:

@Override
    public void beforeRetry(
            @NonNull RetryPolicy retryPolicy,
            @NonNull Retryable<?> retryable,
            @NonNull RetryState retryState

title: Custom WebAuthn Login and Registration Pages in Spring Security
body:
I'd like to add Passkey (WebAuthn) support to an application. As I want to have a custom designed login and registration page, I disable the default registration page and configure a custom login page.

Example using Spring Boot 4.0.0-RC1 with Spring Security 7.0.0-RC1:

@Bean
SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) {
    return http
        .webAuthn($ -> $
            .rpName("Example App")
            .rpId("localhost")
            .allowedOrigins("http://localhost:8080")
            .disableDefaultRegistrationPage(true)
        )
        .formLogin($ -> $.loginPage("/login").permitAll())
        .build();
}

However, when doing so, the JavaScript code Spring Security provides (spring-security-webauthn.js) for client-side WebAuthn operations is no longer available.

Are users expected to implement the client-side WebAuthn logic themselves when using custom login and registration pages? Some reusable JavaScript code would be very helpful to avoid reinventing the wheel for every application and also reduce the risk of (security related) implementation mistakes.

title: How to declare quorum queues with RabbitAmqpAdmin in Spring AMQP 1.0?
body:
I am implementing a messaging solution using Spring Boot and RabbitMQ where our primary requirement is high availability and message safety. Because of this, our goal is to ensure that all queues are created as quorum queues on our RabbitMQ cluster.

We are currently adopting the new AMQP 1.0 support provided by Spring AMQP 4.1 and the next generation client library. Our environment runs RabbitMQ 4 in Docker, configured as a multi-node cluster with the default queue type set to quorum in the configuration file.

In our Spring Boot application, we declare our AMQP 1.0 admin bean and configure the queue using the standard Spring queue builder:

@Bean
public RabbitAmqpAdmin admin(AmqpConnectionFactory connectionFactory) {
    return new RabbitAmqpAdmin(connectionFactory);
}

@Bean
public Queue ordersQueue() {
    return QueueBuilder.durable("orders.processing")
        .quorum()
        .build();
}

When we start the application, the Spring context initializes properly, and the queue is created on the broker without any exceptions. However, when we inspect the newly created queue using the management console, the queue type is reported as classic instead of quorum.

To confirm that our cluster configuration is correct, we tested the exact same queue definition in another project running traditional AMQP 0.9.1 with the standard admin bean. In that project, the queue is created as a quorum queue immediately as expected.

After investigating the decompiled bytecode of the admin class in the AMQP 1.0 library, I noticed that the internal declaration logic unconditionally forces the classic queue specification rather than inspecting the queue arguments for the quorum type. Because it explicitly requests a classic queue, RabbitMQ creates a classic queue even though quorum was requested by the builder.

My questions regarding this behavior are:

  1. Is there an officially supported way to declare quorum queues in AMQP 1.0 without having to write a custom subclass of the admin?

  2. Is this a known limitation in the current release of the client library that will be addressed in an upcoming release?

title: How to preserve custom fields from an OAuth2 token response and use them in Spring Authorization Server JWT generation?
body:
I am integrating a third-party OAuth2 Authorization Code provider with a Spring Security + Spring Authorization Server based application.

The provider supports only OAuth2 Authorization Code Flow and returns opaque access tokens. It does not provide OIDC support or a UserInfo endpoint.

A successful token response looks similar to:

{
  "access_token": "<opaque_access_token>", 
  "refresh_token": "<refresh_token>",  
  "expires_in": 3600,  
  "id": "unique-user-id",  
  "token_type": "bearer"  
}

My application acts as an Authorization Server which supports multiple idps for downstream client applications.

The flow is:

  1. Client initiates authorization with my Authorization Server.

  2. My server delegates authentication to the external OAuth2 provider.

  3. Spring Security performs the authorization-code exchange.

  4. The provider returns the token response shown above.

  5. I need to persist the complete token response in a custom database table.

  6. I also need to preserve the returned "id" value.

  7. Later, when my Authorization Server issues its own JWT access token, I need to use that external "id" as the JWT subject claim.

Example:

{
  "sub": "unique-user-id" 
}

What is the recommended Spring Security / Spring Authorization Server approach for:

  • Accessing custom fields returned in the token response (such as "id")
  • Persisting the token response in a custom database table
  • Making the external "id" available later during JWT generation so it can be used as the "sub" claim

Has anyone implemented a similar integration where identity information is available only in the token response and not through a UserInfo endpoint?

I would like to follow Spring Security and Spring Authorization Server best practices and avoid building custom authentication flows where possible.

title: Spring Security: recommended way to handle per-user permissions with JWT without hitting the DB twice per request?
body:
I'm using Spring Boot 3 / Spring Security 6 with JPA. My JWT contains only the user's email. On every request, my filter loads the User entity from the DB and puts it in the

SecurityContext:

String email = jwtService.extractEmail(token);

var auth = new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(
        user, null, user.getAuthorities());

title: How to add SSL certificates to cacerts and keystore?
body:
I created a CSR file using

openssl req -nodes -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout yourdomain.key -out yourdomain.csr –sha256

It created a CSR file and a key file. I submitted the CSR file to a CA. They responded with a single yourdomain.crt a single file.

I've tried to import the yourdomain.crt to my java's cacert by:

keytool -import -keystore /usr/lib/jvm/java-1.8.0-openjdk-amd64/jre/lib/security/cacerts -file ~/Desktop/user/yourdomain.crt -alias yourdomain

And now I am confused on how to generate a Keystore (jks file). Do I use the same yourdomain.crt? And what is the command that I should use?

My spring boot program consists of 

 File trustStoreFile = new File(CACERTS_PATH);
        File keyStoreFile = new File(JKS_PATH);
        KeyStore ks = KeyStore.getInstance("JKS");
        ks.load(new FileInputStream(keyStoreFile), KEY_PASS.toCharArray());
        return SSLContextBuilder.create()
                .useProtocol("TLS")
                .loadKeyMaterial(ks, KEY_PASS.toCharArray())
                .loadTrustMaterial(trustStoreFile, TRUST_PASS.toCharArray())
                .build();

So I need a cacerts path which I believe is the cacerts from my jdk, and the password is the one which I typed when prompted for it.

Now how do I generate a Keystore file for it?

And do I need to add the server.ssl properties for Spring boot?

title: Spring-Boot Kafka Property-File Configuration
body:
We use Kafka in Spring-Boot 3.4 and we want to upgrade to 4.0

We have some consumers with a Kafka-Listerner annotation. The whole config is in the application yaml-file. We just have the annotation like so:

@Transactional
@KafkaListener(
        topics = "${spring.kafka.consumer.topics.topic1}", 
        groupId = "${spring.kafka.consumer.groups.topic1}", 
        clientIdPrefix = "${spring.kafka.consumer.clients.topic1}",
        containerFactory = "kafkaListenerContainerFactory"
)
void verifyProzessstatus(@Header(KafkaHeaders.RECEIVED_KEY) Long key) {
    businessLogRepository.verify(key);
}

We didn't define any kafkaListenerContainerFactory. This was done be Spring in the background.

Now with the upgrad, Spring doesn't auto provide the kafkaListenerContainerFactory anymore.

I found some code example how to configrue it in the code https://docs.spring.io/spring-kafka/reference/kafka/receiving-messages/listener-annotation.html

I'd prefere to leave the main Kafka config in the application yaml file but I couldn't find any example on how the kafkaListenerContainerFactory would pickup the main kafka config from the file.

And if I would move the whole config to the code, I can't find an example how to define the SSL and SASL stuff in the code.

Here the application.yaml file:

    spring:
      kafka:
        consumer:
          bootstrap-servers: env.kafka.mydomain.org
          topics:
            topic1: my.topic.topic1
          groups:
            topic1: my.group.topic1
          clients:
            topic1: my.topic.topic1
          auto-offset-reset: latest
          key-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer

          enable-auto-commit: true
          isolation-level: read_committed
        jaas:
          enabled: true
          login-module: org.apache.kafka.common.security.scram.ScramLoginModule
          options:
            username: kafka-username
            password: passwd
        security:
          protocol: SASL_SSL
        properties:
          sasl:
            mechanism: SCRAM-SHA-512
        ssl:
          trust-store-type: PEM

title: Spring Boot Callable - 401 Unauthorized: [no body]
body:
I am using Callable interface inside a Spring Boot Application that sends auth request:

public class TestCallable implements Callable<TestDto> {

    TestEntity testEntity;

    public TestCallable(TestEntity testEntity) {
        this.testEntity = testEntity;
    }


    @Override
    public TestDto call() throws Exception {
        String authRequestBody = "{" +
                                    "\"username\": \"" + testEntity.getLogin() + "\"," +
                                    "\"password\": \"" + testEntity.getPassword() + "\"," +
                                    "\"client_id\": \"" + testEntity.getClientId() + "\"," +
                                    "\"client_secret\": \"" + testEntity.getClientSecret() + "\"" +
                                 "}";
        HttpHeaders authHeaders = new HttpHeaders();
        authHeaders.setContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON);
        authHeaders.set("Accept", "application/json");
        authHeaders.set("Grant_type", "password");
        HttpEntity<String> authEntity = new HttpEntity<String>(authRequestBody, authHeaders);
        RestTemplate restTemplate = new RestTemplate();
        TestDto testDto = testDto  = restTemplate.postForObject(testEntity.getEndpoint(), authEntity, TestDto.class);

        return testDto;
    }
}

And I'm sending these requests in 4 threads:

List<Future<TestDto>>  futuresList = new ArrayList<Future<TestDto>>();
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
for (Integer i=0; i<4; i++) {
    Callable<TestDto> callable = new TestCallable(testEntity);
    Future<TestDto> future = pool.submit(callable);
    futuresList.add(future);
}

The issue is that sometimes I get the error "401 Unauthorized: [no body]". For instance, I can receive 4 tokens from 4 callable jobs 5 times and get the error on the 6th attempt.

If I change the number of threads to 2, then I have the error less often. 10 threads fail every time.

And it always works fine in Postman.

How can I understand the cause of the issue?

I am migrating an old Spring Boot 2 app from Java 8 application to Java 11. I did the JPMS migration for javax.xml.bind classes to Java 9 without problems. title: Spring Boot REST server generated with OpenAPI generator doesn't find a Jackson pattern validator for a date-time field generated as an OffsetDateTime
body:
I've received an OpenAPI specification that has rules for the format a date-time can have, regarding milliseconds or microseconds precision especially.

I.e. I have this definition for a date-time field with a millisecond precision:

StartDate:
   type: string
   format: date-time
   pattern: '^[1-2]\d{3}-[0-1]\d-[0-3]\dT[0-2]\d:[0-5]\d:[0-5]\d\.\d{3}Z$'

OpenAPI generator generates some code for a Spring Boot REST server that uses the Java type java.time.OffsetDateTime to handle that date-time:

@Valid @Pattern(regexp = "^[1-2]\\d{3}-[0-1]\\d-[0-3]\\dT[0-2]\\d:[0-5]\\d:[0-5]\\d\\.\\d{3}Z$") 
@Schema(name = "startDate", requiredMode = Schema.RequiredMode.NOT_REQUIRED)
@JsonProperty("startDate")
public @Nullable OffsetDateTime getStartDate() {
    return startDate;
}

However, when executed, the REST server refuses it, as it doesn't find a pattern validator for an OffsetDateTime:

HV000030: No validator could be found for constraint 'jakarta.validation.constraints.Pattern' validating type 'java.time.OffsetDateTime'. Check configuration for 'startDate'

I understand I can recreate the whole validation process following a guide such as this one, but it would be long and complex.

Am I only lacking a Jackson validator dependency that I should have added to my project, but didn't yet, or another declaration if the object mapper, or is there something else that could solve my problem?

title: RAG with Spring AI and Llama 3.2 answers some queries but refuses semantically similar ones
body:
I'm building a RAG pipeline with Spring Boot 3.2, Spring AI 1.0.0, Ollama running Llama 3.2:3b, and pgvector as the vector store. The pipeline retrieves documents from pgvector and injects them into the prompt as context.

The problem: the model refuses to answer some questions and answers others that are semantically very similar. Example:

Query Model response
How many users do I have? "I don't have access to that information."
How many active users do I have? Correct answer with the retrieved context.

This looks like either:

  1. similaritySearch returns no documents (or irrelevant ones) for the first query, and the model falls back to a refusal; or

  2. the model refuses on its own because the system prompt asks it to answer only from the context, and the first query's context is weaker.

My service code:

@Service
public class RagService {

    private final VectorStore vectorStore;
    private final ChatClient chatClient;

    public RagService(VectorStore vectorStore, ChatClient.Builder chatClientBuilder) {
        this.vectorStore = vectorStore;
        this.chatClient = chatClientBuilder.build();
    }

    public String ask(String question) {
        List<Document> docs = vectorStore.similaritySearch(
            SearchRequest.query(question)
                .withTopK(4)
                .withSimilarityThreshold(0.7)
        );
        // I added this log AFTER seeing the issue
        log.info("Retrieved {} docs for query: {}", docs.size(), question);
        docs.forEach(d -> log.info("  -> {}", d.getContent()));

        if (docs.isEmpty()) {
            return "No se encontraron documentos relevantes.";
        }

        String context = docs.stream()
                .map(Document::getContent)
                .collect(Collectors.joining("\n---\n"));

        return chatClient.prompt()
                .system("""
                    You are a helpful assistant. Answer the user's question
                    using ONLY the context below. If the answer is not in the
                    context, say "I don't have access to that information."

                    Context:
                    %s
                    """.formatted(context))
                .user(question)
                .call()
                .content();
    }
}

Configuration (application.yml):

spring:
  ai:
    ollama:
      base-url: http://localhost:11434
      chat:
        options:
          model: llama3.2:3b
          temperature: 0.1
      embedding:
        options:
          model: nomic-embed-text
    vectorstore:
      pgvector:
        index-type: HNSW
        distance-type: COSINE_DISTANCE

What I've already tried:

  • Logging the retrieved documents for both queries. For How many active users do I have? it returns the expected chunk (which mentions "active users"). For How many users do I have? it returns 0 documents even though the same chunk is semantically close.

  • Lowering similarityThreshold from 0.7 to 0.5 → now the first query returns documents, but the model still sometimes refuses.

  • Increasing topK from 4 to 10 → slightly better recall, but still inconsistent.

  • Rephrasing the system prompt to "If the context is not sufficient, answer with what you know and mention the limitation" → the refusal changes but the answer is hallucinated.

  • Running the same query directly in psql with ORDER BY embedding <=> '[…]'::vector LIMIT 4 → returns the same chunk for both queries, so the problem is not the raw SQL.

My questions:

  1. Why would similaritySearch return 0 documents for How many users do I have? but return the correct chunk for How many active users do I have?, when both should be close in embedding space? Is this a known limitation of nomic-embed-text with short queries, of COSINE_DISTANCE + HNSW, or of Spring AI's default threshold behavior?

  2. Is there a recommended way in Spring AI to log or inspect the similarity score of each retrieved document, so I can tune the threshold with data instead of guessing?

  3. Should I preprocess the query (e.g., expand it, or embed a rewritten version) before calling similaritySearch when the user's query is very short?

Versions: Java 21, Spring Boot 3.2.x, Spring AI 1.0.0-M1, Ollama 0.3.x, llama3.2:3b, nomic-embed-text, PostgreSQL 16 with pgvector 0.7.

title: spring.test.database.replace=none does not work as global equivalent of @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
body:
In our Spring Boot 4.1.1 application, all our @SpringBootTest JUnit tests use custom-defined databases with details in the application-test.yml. To make them work we have to disable the attempts to use an "automatic" Spring Boot 4.1.1 database as follows:

@SpringBootTest(classes = { CityStateSP.class })
// NEED TO ADD THIS TO EVERY CLASS: 
// @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
public class CityStateSPTest {

    @Autowired
    private CityStateSP storedProc;

Google AI suggests that the global replacement for this is

spring:
  test:
    database:
      replace: none

But this doesn't work. We've tried multiple variants. application-test.yml contains:

spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: test
  test:
    database:
      replace: none
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:oracle:thin:@<..>
  sql:
    init:
      platform: oracle
      continue-on-error: false

as well as separately at the top,

spring:
  main:
    banner-mode: off
  test:
    database:
      replace: none

Even tried a test/resources/spring.properties containing

spring.test.database.replace=NONE

Any tips? Also, this requirement came in after upgrading to Spring Boot 4.1.1 from 3.5. In Spring Boot 3 there was no requirement for us to have this annotation to have our JUnit tests work.

The test profile is automatically picked up by virtue of Maven-Surefire-Plugin's <spring.profiles.active>test</spring.profiles.active>. I tried adding the disabling of that auto DB there as well, but that didn't work either:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <systemPropertyVariables>

title: What is the correct way to share the result of an Angular Http network call in RxJs 5?

getCustomer() {
    return this.http.get('/someUrl').map(res => res.json());
}

If we take this observable and add multiple subscribers to it:

let network$ = getCustomer();

let subscriber1 = network$.subscribe(...);
let subscriber2 = network$.subscribe(...);

What we want to do, is ensure that this does not cause multiple network requests.

This might seem like an unusual scenario, but its actually quite common: for example if the caller subscribes to the observable to display an error message, and passes it to the template using the async pipe, we already have two subscribers.

What is the correct way of doing that in RxJs 5?

Namely, this seems to work fine:

getCustomer() {
    return this.http.get('/someUrl').map(res => res.json()).share();
}

But is this the idiomatic way of doing this in RxJs 5, or should we do something else instead?

Note : As per Angular 5 new HttpClient, the .map(res => res.json()) part in all examples is now useless, as JSON result is now assumed by default.

title: How to add bootstrap to an angular-cli project

We want to use bootstrap 4 (4.0.0-alpha.2) in our app generated with angular-cli 1.0.0-beta.5 (w/ node v6.1.0).

After getting bootstrap and its dependencies with npm, our first approach consisted in adding them in angular-cli-build.js:

'bootstrap/dist/**/*.min.+(js|css)',  
'jquery/dist/jquery.min.+(js|map)',  
'tether/dist/**/*.min.+(js|css)',

and import them in our index.html

<script src="vendor/jquery/dist/jquery.min.js"></script>
<script src="vendor/tether/dist/js/tether.min.js"></script>
<link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="vendor/bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css">
<script src="vendor/bootstrap/dist/js/bootstrap.min.js"></script>

This worked fine with ng serve but as soon as we produced a build with -prod flag all these dependencies disappeared from dist/vendor (surprise !).

How we are intended to handle such scenario (i.e. loading bootstrap scripts) in a project generated with angular-cli ?

We had the following thoughts but we don't really know which way to go...

  • use a CDN ? but we would rather serve these files to guarantee that they will be available

  • copy dependencies to dist/vendor after our ng build -prod ? But that seems like something angular-cli should provide since it 'takes care' of the build part ?

  • adding jquery, bootstrap and tether in src/system-config.ts and somehow pull them into our bundle in main.ts ? But that seemed wrong considering that we are not going to explicitly use them in our application's code (unlike moment.js or something like lodash, for example).

title: Scheduling access token refresh across tabs
body:
To authenticate users in my Angular app i use access tokens with expiry time X seconds and refresh tokens that can be used to prolong the auth for another X seconds.

So the flow is this:

  • A user signs in. Both the access and refresh tokens are stored in local storage
  • A timer is set (5% shorter than X seconds).
  • When the timer is done, a refresh token request is sent to the server and the local storage is updated with the resulting (new) access and refresh tokens.

My problem is this:

  • If I have multiple tabs open, I will inevitably end up in situations where the refresh is triggered from multiple tabs at the same time. The server will accept the first request, but throw a 400 Bad Request - Invalid refresh token for the subsequent requests, since it considers them used.

Does anyone have a good idea how this could be solved? How does one synchronize things across tabs/windows? I have a couple of ideas but they all seem a bit far fetched:

  • If the response is 400 Bad Request, then retry in a little while (or check if there is a valid updated token already).
  • Try to synchronize the server requests across tabs by posting messages between them.

title: How can Chrome’s built-in PDF viewer download button use a custom filename for an authenticated PDF?
body:
I show a PDF from my backend in an <iframe> using Chrome's built-in PDF viewer. The endpoint requires a bearer token, so Angular fetches the PDF as a Blob and gives the iframe a blob: URL.

The PDF displays correctly, but the viewer's own download icon (and "Save as...") saves it with the blob's UUID, for example cda675a6-10af-42f3-aa68-8795aa8c377d.pdf, instead of the custom name my backend sends.

How can the download button of the native PDF viewer produce the custom file name? A custom download button (<a download>) is not an acceptable fix, because the viewer's own button stays visible and users will keep using it.

Backend (Python/Quart):

@bp.route("/<equipment_id>/equipment_pdf_preview")
@authorization.needs_authorization
async def preview_equipment_pdf_preview(equipment_id, *args, **kwargs):
    equipment = equipments_service.get_by_id(equipment_id)
    if equipment is None:
        return to_response(f"No equipment found with id {equipment_id}", 404)
    pdf = get_equipment_file(equipment_id, watermark_text="IN PLANNING")
    pdf_bytes = pdf.output()
    response = make_response(bytes(pdf_bytes))
    file_name = f"{equipment.name}.pdf"
    response.headers["Content-Type"] = "application/pdf"
    response.headers["Content-Disposition"] = f'inline; filename="{file_name}"'
    response.headers["Access-Control-Expose-Headers"] = "Content-Disposition"
    return response

Angular service (simplified):

getPdfPreview(id: number): Observable<Blob> {
  return this.http.get(`${this.baseUrl}/${id}/equipment_pdf_preview`, { responseType: 'blob' });
}

Angular component:

viewPdf(equipment_id: number): void {
  this.equipmentService.getPdfPreview(equipment_id).subscribe({
    next: (blob: Blob) => {
      this.pdfBlob = blob;
      const objectUrl = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
      this.pdfUrl = this.sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustResourceUrl(objectUrl);
    },
    error: (err) => {
      console.error(err);
      this.pdfUrl = null;
      this.snackbar.open('Failed to load PDF preview.', 'Okay', { duration: 2500 });
    },
  });
}

Template (simplified):

<iframe [src]="pdfUrl" width="100%" height="800"></iframe>

What I observed:

  • In DevTools > Network, the response has the correct Content-Disposition. With observe: 'response', Angular also reads the right file name, so the header is not lost on the way to Angular.
  • The viewer's toolbar title and its download name are the blob UUID.
  • As far as I can tell from Chromium's pdf_viewer.ts, the viewer takes the file name from the URL it loaded and ignores the query and fragment. Because it is only given blob:http://.../<uuid>, it never sees the header. Is that understanding correct?

I tried:

  1. Header plus Access-Control-Expose-Headers, read in Angular (above). The name reaches Angular, but it has no effect on the viewer.
  2. Service worker + Cache API serving a fake URL ending in the file name, as in the top answer to Can I set the filename of a PDF object displayed in Chrome?. The viewer shows the right name, but clicking its download button offers an .htm document instead of a PDF. That answer's own edit and comments report the same: the worker never sees the download request. This matches Chromium issue 40410035, where the fetch event does not fire for browser-initiated downloads.

Is there any way to make Chrome's built-in PDF viewer use a custom file name for its own download button when the PDF can only be fetched with an Authorization header?

If it is impossible with blob URLs, what is the recommended way to serve this PDF from a real URL whose last path segment is the file name, while keeping Bearer authentication and without a custom download button? For example, a short-lived signed URL or a scoped cookie. What pitfalls should I expect, such as the viewer requesting the URL again on download, or range requests?

Can I set the filename of a PDF object displayed in Chrome? and Set the default save as name for a an <embed> or <iframe> that uses a Blob say it is impossible with blob URLs or suggest the service worker trick, which fails on the viewer's download button. They do not cover an authenticated endpoint, where an iframe cannot send the Authorization header.

title: Is there a way to know when an msal redirect is in progress?
body:
I'm using the @azure/msal-browser and @azure/msal-angular packages in order to simply retrieve an MSAL token for my signed in users. Since all I really need is the token, I have only provided the MsalService and MSAL_INSTANCE in my app.module.ts. I am using the redirect flow and have chosen to subscribe to the .handleRedirectObservable() method myself instead of using the MsalRedirectComponent (so that I know exactly when the token is available).

My problem is that when the redirect happens and I am forwarded back to my application there is a period of time where my app is running but the redirect interaction still hasn't quite finished. If I allow my app to actually start running at this point, there is a chance that it will try to use the token before it is truly there and cause errors. So instead I am having to define a method called isInteractionInProgress and call that in my app.component.ts before actually starting execution of my app:

  public isInteractionInProgress(): boolean {
    for (let i = 0; i < sessionStorage.length; i+= 1) {
      if (sessionStorage.getItem(sessionStorage.key(i)) === 'interaction_in_progress') {
        return true;
      }
    }
    return false;
  }

Since I don't know a reliable way to generate the key that the msal-angular library uses to store the 'interaction_in_progress' value, I'm having to iterate through the session storage myself and look for this key. If it exists then my app knows an MSAL token is on the way and it needs to wait.

Is there a better solution for this? It almost seems like this is supposed to be doing what I need:

this.msalBroadcastService.inProgress$
      .pipe(
        filter((status: InteractionStatus) => status === InteractionStatus.None),
        takeUntil(this._destroying$)
      )
      .subscribe(() => {
        // Do user account/UI functions here
      })

But all it does is activate on 'none' twice and the second 'none' seems to be when the token is actually available but I'm not sure if that is true.

Is there a reliable way to know when the redirect is actually happening?

title: Nested resource handling in new data fetching with resources approach
body:
Data fetching with resources introduces a new way of resolve data while routing.

I want to reuse loaded data from parent route. With old resource data resolver it works well using following code:

export const purchaseOrdersResolver: ResolveFn<PurchaseOrder[]> = (route: ActivatedRouteSnapshot, state: RouterStateSnapshot) => {
  let purchaseOrderService: PurchaseOrderService = inject(PurchaseOrderService);
  return purchaseOrderService.getPurchaseOrders();
};

export const purchaseOrderResolver: ResolveFn<PurchaseOrder> = (route: ActivatedRouteSnapshot, state: RouterStateSnapshot) => {
  const router = inject(Router);
  const purchaseOrderId: number|null = route.paramMap.get('purchaseId') as number|null;
  if (purchaseOrderId != null) {
    const purchaseOrders = route.data['purchaseOrders'] as PurchaseOrder[];
    const purchaseOrder: PurchaseOrder|undefined = purchaseOrders.find(i => i.id == purchaseOrderId);
    if (purchaseOrder) {
      return purchaseOrder;
    }
  }
  return of(new RedirectCommand(router.parseUrl('/po')));
};


export const poRoute: Route = {
  path: "po",
  title: "Purchase orders"
  resolve: { purchaseOrders: purchaseOrdersResolver },
  children: [
    {
        path: "",
        component: PurchaseOrderListComponent,
        title: "Purchase orders"
    },
    {
        path: ":purchaseId",
        component: PurchaseOrderOverviewComponent,
        title: "Purchase orders",
        resolve: { purchaseOrder: purchaseOrderResolver }
    },
  ]
};

Using the new resource API, first parts of my code look like:

export function fetchPurchaseOrdersObservable(purchaseOrderService: PurchaseOrderService): Observable<PurchaseOrder[]>  {
  return purchaseOrderService.getPurchaseOrders();
}

export function fetchPurchaseOrderObservable(purchaseOrderId: number, router: Router): Observable<PurchaseOrder> {
  if (purchaseOrderId != null) {
    const purchaseOrders = ?? as PurchaseOrder[];
    const purchaseOrder: PurchaseOrder|undefined = purchaseOrders.find(i => i.id == purchaseOrderId);
    if (purchaseOrder) {
      return purchaseOrder;
    }
  }
  throw new RedirectCommand(router.parseUrl('/purchase-order'));
}

export const poRoute: Route = {
  path: "po",
  title: "Purchase orders"
  resources: (ctx) => {
    const purchaseOrderService: PurchaseOrderService = inject(PurchaseOrderService);
    return {
      purchaseOrders: rxResource({
        stream: () => fetchPurchaseOrdersObservable(purchaseOrderService),
      })
    }
  },
  children: [
    {
        path: "",
        component: PurchaseOrderListComponent,
        title: "Purchase orders"
    },
    {
        path: ":purchaseId",
        component: PurchaseOrderOverviewComponent,
        title: "Purchase orders",
        resources: (ctx) => {
            const router = inject(Router);
            return {
                purchaseOrder: rxResource({
                    params: () => ctx.params()['purchaseOrderId'],
                    stream: ({params: [purchaseOrderId]}) => fetchPurchaseOrderObservable(purchaseOrderId, router),
                })
            }),
        }
    },
  ]
};

What is the right way of receiving results from fetchPurchaseOrdersObservable() in fetchPurchaseOrderObservable() without interacting with the backend again? Is there a new way in Angular 22 to access nested data as replacement of route.data[...] (even if Parallel execution is considered)?

title: Angular NGRX selectors with parameter

This model comes from store and in my child component I want to transform it to a view model that will reflect my template needs.

selectEntityViewModel = (id:string) => createSelector(selectEntityById(id), ()=>  
 return { /* here transform entity selected into view model and return  */ })

entity = input.required<Entity>();

I got around this problem by first getting all entities, and then selecting each of parameter from it using computed functions:

title: How do I successfully return httpResource from a function in a service?
body:
I have an existing Angular app (pre v19) that we have migrated to 22.1.6. In the current version of the app, we use traditional httpClient.get calls in a service and subscribe to them in the component. Now that we are on a version with a stable httpResource, we want to replace the httpClient calls with that and implement signals. We prefer to maintain the structure of having the API calls in a service because several of them get called from multiple components and we do not want to duplicate code.

I always get a resource that is loading and has no data. (I know that I really need to just pass the accountId as a number signal and pass it to params and eventually I will. I know that the API is working because I can call it using httpClient and the first form above of httpResource and everything is good.     Vue.use(Router)

    export default new Router({
        routes: [
            {
                path: '/',
                name: 'Hello',
                component: Hello
            }
        ]
    })

I've not seen the at sign (@) in a path before. I suspect it allows for relative paths (maybe?) but I wanted to be sure I understand what it truly does.

What does the @ do in this path (link to documentation would be fantastic) and is this an es6 thing? A webpack thing? A vue-loader thing?

UPDATE

Thanks, Felix Kling for pointing me to another duplicate stackoverflow question/answer about this same question.

While the comment on the other stackoverflow post isn't the exact answer to this question (it wasn't a babel plugin in my case) it did point me in the correct direction to find what it was.

In the scaffolding that vue-cli cranks out for you, part of the base webpack config sets up an alias for .vue files:

This makes sense both in the fact that it gives you a relative path from the src file and it removes the requirement of the .vue at the end of the import path (which you normally need).

Thanks for the help!

title: Difference between the created and mounted events in Vue.js
body:
Vue.js documentation describes the created and mounted events as follows:

created

Called synchronously after the instance is created. At this stage, the instance has finished processing the options which means the following have been set up: data observation, computed properties, methods, watch/event callbacks. However, the mounting phase has not been started, and the $el property will not be available yet.

mounted

Called after the instance has just been mounted where el is replaced by the newly created vm.$el. If the root instance is mounted to an in-document element, vm.$el will also be in-document when mounted is called.

This hook is not called during server-side rendering.

I understand the theory, but I have 2 questions regarding practice:

  2. What can I use the created event for, in real-life (real-code) situation?

title: `ref()` vs `reactive()` in Vue 3?

One example each from the ones I looked at:

For reactive()

<template>
  <button @click="increment">
    Count is: {{ state.count }}, double is: {{ state.double }}
  </button>
</template>

<script>
import { reactive, computed } from 'vue'

export default {
  setup() {
    const state = reactive({
      count: 0,
      double: computed(() => state.count * 2)
    })

    function increment() {
      state.count++
    }

    return {
      state,
      increment
    }
  }
}
</script>

For ref()

<template>
  <div>
    <h2 ref="titleRef">{{ formattedMoney }}</h2>
    <input v-model="delta" type="number">
    <button @click="add">Add</button>
  </div>
</template>

<script>
import { ref, computed, onMounted } from "vue";

title: How to watch props change with Vue Composition API / Vue 3?
body:
While Vue Composition API RFC Reference site has many advanced use scenarios with the watch module, there are no examples of how to watch component props.

Neither is it mentioned in Vue Composition API RFC's main page or vuejs/composition-api in Github.

I've created a Codesandbox to elaborate on this issue.

<template>
  <div id="app">
    <img width="25%" src="./assets/logo.png">
    <br>
    <p>Prop watch demo with select input using v-model:</p>
    <PropWatchDemo :selected="testValue"/>
  </div>
</template>

<script>
import { createComponent, onMounted, ref } from "@vue/composition-api";
import PropWatchDemo from "./components/PropWatchDemo.vue";

export default createComponent({
  name: "App",
  components: {
    PropWatchDemo
  },
  setup: (props, context) => {
    const testValue = ref("initial");

    onMounted(() => {
      setTimeout(() => {
        console.log("Changing input prop value after 3s delay");
        testValue.value = "changed";
        // This value change does not trigger watchers?
      }, 3000);
    });

    return {
      testValue
    };
  }
});
</script>

<template>
  <select v-model="selected">
    <option value="null">null value</option>
    <option value>Empty value</option>
  </select>
</template>

<script>
import { createComponent, watch } from "@vue/composition-api";

export default createComponent({
  name: "MyInput",
  props: {
    selected: {
      type: [String, Number],
      required: true
    }
  },
  setup(props) {
    console.log("Setup props:", props);

    watch((first, second) => {
      console.log("Watch function called with args:", first, second);
      // First arg function registerCleanup, second is undefined
    });

    // watch(props, (first, second) => {
    //   console.log("Watch props function called with args:", first, second);
    //   // Logs error:
    //   // Failed watching path: "[object Object]" Watcher only accepts simple
    //   // dot-delimited paths. For full control, use a function instead.
    // })

    watch(props.selected, (first, second) => {
      console.log(
        "Watch props.selected function called with args:",
        first,
        second
      );
      // Both props are undefined so it's just a bare callback func to be run
    });

    return {};
  }
});
</script>

Although my question and code example were initially with JavaScript, I'm using TypeScript. Tony Tom's first answer although working, led to a type error. Which was solved by Michal Levý's answer. So I've tagged this question with typescript afterward.

Here is my polished yet barebones version of the reactive wirings for this custom select component, on top of <b-form-select> from bootstrap-vue (otherwise agnostic-implementation but this underlying component does emit @input and @change events both, based on whether the change was made programmatically or by user interaction).

<template>
  <b-form-select
    v-model="selected"
    :options="{}"
    @input="handleSelection('input', $event)"
    @change="handleSelection('change', $event)"
  />
</template>

<script lang="ts">
import {
  createComponent, SetupContext, Ref, ref, watch, computed,
} from '@vue/composition-api';

interface Props {
  value?: string | number | boolean;
}

export default createComponent({
  name: 'CustomSelect',
  props: {
    value: {
      type: [String, Number, Boolean],
      required: false, // Accepts null and undefined as well
    },
  },
  setup(props: Props, context: SetupContext) {
    // Create a Ref from prop, as two-way binding is allowed only with sync -modifier,
    // with passing prop in parent and explicitly emitting update event on child:
    // Ref: https://v2.vuejs.org/v2/guide/components-custom-events.html#sync-Modifier
    // Ref: https://medium.com/@jithilmt/vue-js-2-two-way-data-binding-in-parent-and-child-components-1cd271c501ba
    const selected: Ref<Props['value']> = ref(props.value);

    const handleSelection = function emitUpdate(type: 'input' | 'change', value: Props['value']) {
      // For sync -modifier where 'value' is the prop name
      context.emit('update:value', value);
      // For @input and/or @change event propagation
      // @input emitted by the select component when value changed <programmatically>
      // @change AND @input both emitted on <user interaction>
      context.emit(type, value);
    };

    // Watch prop value change and assign to value 'selected' Ref
    watch(() => props.value, (newValue: Props['value']) => {
      selected.value = newValue;
    });

    return {
      selected,
      handleSelection,
    };
  },
});
</script>

How do these compare to each other, to be more specific than declared in Vue docs?

A Tip on Sass Performance

Note that when using Dart Sass, synchronous compilation is twice as fast as asynchronous compilation by default, due to the overhead of asynchronous callbacks. To avoid this overhead, you can use the fibers package to call asynchronous importers from the synchronous code path. To enable this, simply install fibers as a project dependency:

npm install -D fibers

Please also be aware, as it's a native module, there may be compatibility issues vary on the OS and build environment. In that case, please run npm uninstall -D fibers to fix the problem.

? Pick a CSS pre-processor (PostCSS, Autoprefixer and CSS Modules are supported by default): (Use arrow keys)
❯ Sass/SCSS (with dart-sass)
  Sass/SCSS (with node-sass)
  Less
  Stylus

EDIT 2020/01: Vue CLI 4.2.2 create new project is still suggesting dart-sass as the first option before node-sass. Yet it has been established here that node-sass is the more performant choice, and almost nobody uses dart-sass (ccleve's comment).

EDIT 2020/09: As Ali Bahrami updated his extensive answer, dart-sass is the preferred choice as node-sass is being marked as deprecated.

Too bad dart-sass in it's a JS-compiled version has poor performance. However, it's developers are well aware of this, and are working towards greater performance as stated in this issue.

title: Communication between sibling components in Vue.js 2.0
body:
Overview

In Vue.js 2.x, model.sync will be deprecated.

So, what is a proper way to communicate between sibling components in Vue.js 2.x?

Background

As I understand Vue.js 2.x, the preferred method for sibling communication is to use a store or an event bus.

According to Evan (creator of Vue.js):

It's also worth mentioning "passing data between components" is generally a bad idea, because in the end the data flow becomes untrackable and very hard to debug.

If a piece of data needs to be shared by multiple components, prefer global stores or Vuex.

[Link to discussion]

And:

.once and .sync are deprecated. Props are now always one-way down. To produce side effects in the parent scope, a component needs to explicitly emit an event instead of relying on implicit binding.

So, Evan suggests using $emit() and $on().

Concerns

What worries me is:

  • Each store and event has a global visibility (correct me if I'm wrong);
  • It's too wasteful to create a new store for each minor communication;

What I want is to some scope events or stores visibility for siblings components. (Or perhaps I didn't understand the above idea.)

Question

So, what is the correct way to communicate between sibling components?

export class PhoneMaskDirective {

  constructor(public ngControl: NgControl) { }

  @HostListener('ngModelChange', ['$event'])
  onModelChange(event) {
    this.onInputChange(event, false);
  }

  @HostListener('keydown.backspace', ['$event'])
  keydownBackspace(event) {
    this.onInputChange(event.target.value, true);
  }


  onInputChange(event, backspace) {
    let newVal = event.replace(/\D/g, '');
    if (backspace && newVal.length <= 6) {
      newVal = newVal.substring(0, newVal.length - 1);
    }
    if (newVal.length === 0) {
      newVal = '';
    } else if (newVal.length <= 3) {
      newVal = newVal.replace(/^(\d{0,3})/, '$1');
    } else if (newVal.length <= 6) {
      newVal = newVal.replace(/^(\d{0,3})(\d{0,3})/, '$1 $2');
    } else if (newVal.length <= 9) {
      newVal = newVal.replace(/^(\d{0,3})(\d{0,3})(\d{0,4})/, '$1 $2 $3');
    } else {
      newVal = newVal.substring(0, 10);
      newVal = newVal.replace(/^(\d{0,3})(\d{0,3})(\d{0,4})/, '$1 $2 $3');

title: Vue.js - Making helper functions globally available to single-file components
body:
I have a Vue 2 project that has many (50+) single-file components. I use Vue-Router for routing and Vuex for state.

There is a file, called helpers.js, that contains a bunch of general-purpose functions, such as capitalizing the first letter of a string. This file looks like this:

export default {
  capitalizeFirstLetter(str) {
    return str.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + str.slice(1);
  }
}

My main.js file initializes the app:

import Vue from 'vue'
import VueResource from "vue-resource"
import store from "./store"
import Router from "./router"
import App from "./components/App.vue"

Vue.use(VueResource)

const app = new Vue({
  router: Router,
  store,
  template: '<app></app>',
  components: { App },
}).$mount('#app')

My App.vue file contains the template:

<template>
  <navbar></navbar>
  <div class="container">
    <router-view></router-view>
  </div>
</template>

<script>
export default {
  data() {
    return {
      // stuff
    }
  }
}
</script>

I then have a bunch of single-file components, which Vue-Router handles navigating to inside the <router-view> tag in the App.vue template.

Now let's say that I need to use the capitalizeFirstLetter() function inside a component that is defined in SomeComponent.vue. In order to do this, I first need to import it:

<template>Some Component</template>

<script>
import {capitalizeFirstLetter} from '../helpers.js'
export default {
  data() {
    return {
      myString = "test"
    }
  },
  created() {
    var newString = this.capitalizeFirstLetter(this.myString)
  }
}
</script>

This becomes a problem quickly because I end up importing the function into many different components, if not all of them. This seems repetitive and also makes the project harder to maintain. For example if I want to rename helpers.js, or the functions inside it, I then need to go into every single component that imports it and modify the import statement.

Long story short: how do I make the functions inside helpers.js globally available so that I can call them inside any component without having to first import them and then prepend this to the function name? I basically want to be able to do this:

<script>
export default {
  data() {
    return {
      myString = "test"
    }
  },
  created() {
    var newString = capitalizeFirstLetter(this.myString)
  }
}
</script>

title: Is there a proper way of resetting a component's initial data in vuejs?
body:
I have a component with a specific set of starting data:

data: function (){
    return {
        modalBodyDisplay: 'getUserInput', // possible values: 'getUserInput', 'confirmGeocodedValue'
        submitButtonText: 'Lookup', // possible values 'Lookup', 'Yes'
        addressToConfirm: null,
        bestViewedByTheseBounds: null,
        location:{
            name: null,
            address: null,
            position: null
        }
}

This is data for a modal window, so when it shows I want it to start with this data. If the user cancels from the window I want to reset all of the data to this.

I know I can create a method to reset the data and just manually set all of the data properties back to their original:

reset: function (){
    this.modalBodyDisplay = 'getUserInput';
    this.submitButtonText = 'Lookup';
    this.addressToConfirm = null;
    this.bestViewedByTheseBounds = null;
    this.location = {
        name: null,
        address: null,
        position: null
    };
}

But this seems really sloppy. It means that if I ever make a change to the component's data properties I'll need to make sure I remember to update the reset method's structure. That's not absolutely horrible since it's a small modular component, but it makes the optimization portion of my brain scream.

The solution that I thought would work would be to grab the initial data properties in a ready method and then use that saved data to reset the components:

data: function (){
    return {
        modalBodyDisplay: 'getUserInput', 
        submitButtonText: 'Lookup', 
        addressToConfirm: null,
        bestViewedByTheseBounds: null,
        location:{
            name: null,
            address: null,
            position: null
        },
        // new property for holding the initial component configuration
        initialDataConfiguration: null
    }
},
ready: function (){
    // grabbing this here so that we can reset the data when we close the window.
    this.initialDataConfiguration = this.$data;
},
methods:{
    resetWindow: function (){
        // set the data for the component back to the original configuration
        this.$data = this.initialDataConfiguration;
    }
}

But the initialDataConfiguration object is changing along with the data (which makes sense because in the read method our initialDataConfiguration is getting the scope of the data function.

Is there a way of grabbing the initial configuration data without inheriting the scope?

Am I overthinking this and there's a better/easier way of doing this?

Is hardcoding the initial data the only option?

title: How to use ESLint for vue template placed in separate html file
body:
Imagine you have "SFC" with template like this:

<template src="./my-separate.html"></template>
<script>/* whatever */</script>
<style>/* whatever */</style>

And imagine you have working prettier/eslint setup and you can lint any of your files with such command:

eslint --ext "*.html, *.js, *.vue, *.ts" $FilePath$ --fix --no-ignore

Which formats .vue, .js or even .ts file pretty fine, but if you use it against your separated vue-template - which is a file with .html extension, but it's actually vue template with all v-ifs and other stuff... This won't work because prettier probably trying to parse .html with incorrect parser (?) or maybe there is should be a way to suggest which parser to use for my tricky .html files?

My current configs looks like this:

// .prettier.rc

{
  "arrowParens": "always",
  "semi": false,
  "singleQuote": true
}

// .eslintrc.js

module.exports = {
  root: true,
  parserOptions: {
    parser: 'typescript-eslint-parser',
    sourceType: 'module',
    jsx: true
  },
  env: {
    browser: true
  },
  extends: [
    'eslint:recommended',
    'plugin:prettier/recommended',
    'prettier/vue',
    'plugin:vue/recommended'
  ],

  plugins: [
    'typescript',
    // required to lint *.vue files
    'vue',
    'prettier'
  ]
}

And versions of some libraries used:

"babel-eslint": "8.2.6",
"eslint": "5.11.1",
"eslint-config-prettier": "3.3.0",
"eslint-friendly-formatter": "4.0.1",
"eslint-loader": "2.1.1",
"eslint-plugin-import": "2.14.0",
"eslint-plugin-node": "8.0.0",
"eslint-plugin-prettier": "3.0.0",
"eslint-plugin-promise": "^4.0.1",
"eslint-plugin-standard": "^4.0.0",
"eslint-plugin-typescript": "0.14.0",
"eslint-plugin-vue": "5.0.0",

Maybe someone can give me the cue how to format with prettier/eslint .html files with vue-specific templates inside?

Currently for .html I have neither IDE errors nor autoformatting, but for everything else (.vue, .js, .ts files) it works fine.

For the command I mentioned I can see eslint uses parser-babylon and reasonably complains against the first vue-related thing, e.g. :prop binding.

UPD: from my experience if you're trying to extract vue-template to HTML you're already doing something wrong. It's a way to avoid template copy-pasting, but you actually will create N identical components with that approach (if you reuse that HTML chunk in N SFCs). So you better embrace SFC and try to make a reusable component instead of having a reusable HTML file. In that way, you won't have any issues with linting too.

title: How to generate a form based on a configuration and retrieve all values from it on submit?
body:
When launching my Vue 3 app it asks for a configuration from an external API. This returns an array of

interface FieldConfig {
  fieldId: string;
  dataType: 'string' | 'boolean' | 'number';
  defaultValueFunction?: () => Promise<unknown> | unknown;
}

Based on those field configurations I want to create a form ( where each dataType decides which input to render ) and whenever I click the submit button I want the form to collect all the field values so I can add them as a payload to a POST request body.

Since everything should be reactive and the communication should be bidirectional I'm struggling to create a form with v-models out of nowhere so I started with a basic component rendering the a single input

FormField.vue

<script setup lang="ts">
import { FieldConfig } from "./FieldConfig.ts";

defineProps<{
  fieldConfiguration: FieldConfig;
  fieldValue: boolean | string | number | null | undefined
}>();

const emit = defineEmits<{
  (e: "update:modelValue", newValue: boolean | string | number | null | undefined): void;
}>();

function emitNewValue(newValue: boolean | string | number | null | undefined) {
  emit("update:modelValue", newValue);
}
</script>

<template>
  <v-checkbox v-if="fieldConfiguration.dataType === 'boolean'" label="boolean" :model-value="fieldValue" @update:modelValue="emitNewValue" />
  <v-text-field v-else-if="fieldConfiguration.dataType === 'number'" type="number" label="number or null" :model-value="fieldValue" clearable @update:modelValue="emitNewValue" />
  <v-text-field v-else-if="fieldConfiguration.dataType === 'string'" label="string or null" :model-value="fieldValue" clearable @update:modelValue="emitNewValue" />
</template>

Now the tricky part: I created a form that must be able to hold all the field values based on the props ( holding the field configurations ). You will see that I created a local ref variable holding all the form values. I initialize the variable inside the onMounted hook

CreateForm.vue

<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref, onMounted } from "vue";
import { FieldConfig } from "./FieldConfig.ts";
import FormField from "./FormField.vue";

const props = defineProps<{
  fieldConfigurations: FieldConfig[]
}>();

const emit = defineEmits<{
  (e: "create", payload: Record<string, unknown>): void;
}>();

const createForm = ref<VForm>();
const payload: [string, unknown][] = ref([]);

onMounted(() => {
  resetForm();
});

function create() {
  let payloadAsRecord: Record<string, unknown> = {};

  payload.value.forEach(([fieldId, fieldValue]) => {
        payloadAsRecord[fieldId] = fieldValue;
  });

  emit("create", payloadAsRecord);
  
  resetForm();
}

function onValueChanged(fieldId: string, newValue: unknown) {
  payload.value = payload.value.map(([currentFieldId, currentFieldValue]) => {
    if(currentFieldId === fieldId) {
        return [currentFieldId, newValue];  
    }
    
    return [currentFieldId, currentFieldValue];
  });
}

/* async */ function resetForm() {
  payload.value = props.fieldConfigurations.map(fieldConfiguration => {
    let initialValue = null;
    
    if(fieldConfiguration.dataType === 'boolean') {
      initialValue = false;
    }
    
    // call async defaultValueFunction if defined
    
    return [fieldConfiguration.fieldId, initialValue];
  });
}
</script>

<template>
    <v-card>
      <v-card-text>
        <v-form ref="createForm">
          <form-field
            v-for="([fieldId, fieldValue], fieldIndex) in payload"
            :key="fieldIndex"
            :fieldConfiguration="fieldConfigurations.find(fieldConfig => fieldConfig.fieldId === fieldId)!"
            :fieldValue="fieldValue"
            @update:modelValue="onValueChanged(fieldId, $event)"
          />
        </v-form>
      </v-card-text>
      <v-card-actions>
        <v-spacer />
        <v-btn @click="create">Submit</v-btn>
      </v-card-actions>
    </v-card>
</template>

For testing purposes I consume this form component with the following mock data

const fieldConfigurations: Ref<FieldConfig[]> = ref([
  { fieldId: 'field-1', dataType: 'boolean' },
  { fieldId: '2', dataType: 'string', defaultValueFunction: () => 'foo' },
  { fieldId: 'numeric', dataType: 'number', defaultValueFunction: async () => {
    await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 1000));
    
    return 42;
  }}
]);

You can play around with the code here

I would like to know if there are any better ways to solve this. I think the component runs into troubles whenever the props change because the onMounted hook does not run again.

And maybe I don't even know the local payload ref variable because this can be solved "smarter"... I basically want to generate a form based on the field configurations and ask the form for all values whenever I want to submit them.

                comp.playVideo(url);

            }
        },

            this.$emit('added-message', this);

        },

            if (input.files && input.files[0]) {
                let fileReader = new FileReader();
                fileReader.onload = function () {
                    callback(fileReader.result);
                };
                fileReader.readAsDataURL(input.files[0]);
            }
            else {
                callback(null);
            }
        },

        // Read a file input as an object url.
        readObjectUrl(input, callback) {
            if (input.files && input.files[0]) {
                let fileReader = new FileReader();
                fileReader.onload = function () {
                    let blob = new Blob([fileReader.result], {type: input.files[0].type});
                    let url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
                    callback(url, blob);
                };
                fileReader.readAsArrayBuffer(input.files[0]);
            }
            else {
                callback(null);
            }

        },

    }

}

and a click handler that passes the appropriate locale to a method:

setLocale(locale) {
  this.$root.$i18n.locale = locale;
},

where VueI18n is defined here:

import Vue from 'vue';
import VueI18n from 'vue-i18n';

Vue.use(VueI18n);

function loadLocaleMessages() {
  const locales = require.context('./locales', true, /[A-Za-z0-9-_,\s]+\.json$/i);
  const messages = {};
  locales.keys().forEach((key) => {
    const matched = key.match(/([A-Za-z0-9-_]+)\./i);
    if (matched && matched.length > 1) {
      const locale = matched[1];
      messages[locale] = locales(key);
    }
  });
  return messages;
}

export default new VueI18n({
  locale: 'en',
  localeDir: 'locales',
  fallbackLocale: 'en',
  messages: loadLocaleMessages(),
});

I've also tried variations, such as 

this.$i18n.locale = locale;

and 

i18n.locale = locale;

after also doing

import i18n from `@/i18n';

in the component. However, almost none of them change all of my field name values that have translations. It's almost as if I have to force a re-render of my translated values once the language has been changed.

Is there something different I need to do in order to get all of my translated values to update once I have selected a different language?
